course.title: Engineering: Structures and Machines
course.description: Load a beam, find the forces in a truss, size a section and gear a hoist. The statics and strength of materials behind real structures.
course.audience: An adult comfortable with algebra and basic trigonometry who knows forces, Newton's laws, work and energy, as in Physics: Motion and Forces.

paragraphs: Engineering of structures and machines starts with one habit. Take something that has to stay up or has to move, work out the forces on it, and check that it can take them. People study it because every bridge, crane, shelf and gearbox has to pass that check before anyone builds it, and most of the check is arithmetic you can learn.

The course has twelve lessons in four parts. Loads and equilibrium covers splitting forces, turning effects and the forces at the supports of a beam. Structures finds the force in each bar of a truss, then the stress a bar can carry. Beams and stiffness looks inside a loaded beam, at the shear and bending in it and how far it sags. Machines finishes with levers, pulleys, gears, efficiency and power.
Each lesson follows one object, such as a post with ropes tied to it or a steel rod under load, and explains an idea before it asks about it.
outcomes: You'll be able to split a slanted force into parts and find the force that balances a set of forces.
You'll be able to find the reactions at the supports of a loaded beam.
You'll be able to work out the force in each member of a simple truss and say whether it is pulled or pushed.
You'll be able to turn a load into a stress, and a stress into a stretch.
You'll be able to find the speed, force and power at the output of a lever, pulley or gear train.

lessons.title: Forces as vectors

lead.text: Take the post in the yard and start with the simplest arrangement, in which every rope runs along one straight line. Each pull has a size and a direction. We measure size in newtons, and because structures carry big loads we use kilonewtons (kN) instead, where 1 kN is 1,000 N, about the weight of a 100 kg load.

When two people pull the same way, their efforts team up and the sizes add. If one pulls with 6 kN and the other with 2 kN, the post feels 8 kN in that direction. If the second person pulls the opposite way instead, the two pulls fight each other and the post feels only the difference. Both cases are in the picture below.

afterFigure.text: Adding and subtracting is all we need while everything lies on one line, and that is also where the method stops. A rope that runs off at a slant cannot simply be added, because only part of its pull acts in any one direction. The next few screens deal with exactly that.

lead.text: Use what the last screen showed about pulls on a single line.

Now tie a rope to the top of the post and run it to a hook on a tall tree, some way off and higher up. The rope pulls the post towards the tree, and it also pulls the post upwards. One rope is doing two jobs at once.

We can describe that pull in two pieces. One piece acts across, along the horizontal, and the other acts up, along the vertical. The two pieces are at right angles to each other, and together they have exactly the effect of the original pull. Each piece is called a component of the force. A component is the same pull described in two parts, with nothing extra added. The picture below shows the pieces for two different slants.

afterFigure.text: The angle is measured up from the horizontal. The steeper the rope, the larger the upward piece and the smaller the sideways piece. A rope lying flat along the ground has no upward piece at all, and a rope pulling straight up has no sideways piece. The next screen turns this into numbers.

lead.text: To put numbers on the two pieces, draw the force as the sloping side of a right-angled triangle. The across piece lies along the horizontal side and the up piece along the upright side.

Trigonometry links those sides to the angle θ (theta), measured from the horizontal. The side that touches the angle carries the cosine of θ, so the across piece is F cos θ. The side opposite the angle carries the sine of θ, so the up piece is F sin θ. In both, F is the size of the whole force.

afterFigure.text: Try it on a rope pulling with 8 kN at 45°. The across piece is 8 × cos 45° = 5.66 kN and the up piece is 8 × sin 45° = 5.66 kN. They are equal because 45° sits exactly halfway between flat and upright. Put your calculator in degrees mode before you try your own.

lead.text: Here is the whole method for a steeper rope, with the reason for each line.

workedSteps.text: The horizontal side touches the angle, so use cosine.
The vertical side is opposite the angle, so use sine.
Check: the parts combine back to the original force.

steps.headline: Reading a slope instead of an angle

lead.text: Drawings of real structures often give a slope instead of an angle, such as a cable that rises 3 m for every 4 m it runs across. A slope like that is already a right-angled triangle, with the rise as the upright side and the run as the flat side. The cable itself is the sloping side.

Pythagoras gives its length: √(3² + 4²) = 5. The sine and cosine are only ratios of sides, so the up piece is the force times rise ÷ length and the across piece is the force times run ÷ length. A 10 kN pull on that cable has an up piece of 10 × 3/5 = 6 kN and an across piece of 10 × 4/5 = 8 kN, with no calculator needed.

afterFigure.text: The shortcut works whenever the sides come out as whole numbers, as with 3, 4, 5 or 5, 12, 13. When they do not, fall back on the angle and your calculator.

steps.headline: A 5 kN cable pull runs along a line that rises 3 m for every 4 m across. Find its vertical component.

lead.text: Same method as the last screen, now on a smaller pull.

workedSteps.text: Find the long side of the slope triangle.
The vertical share is the rise over the long side.
Multiply the pull by that share, in kN.

lead.text: Splitting a force is half the job. The other half is putting forces back together. Suppose one person pulls the post east with 8 kN and another pulls it north with 15 kN. The post feels a single combined pull, called the resultant: the one force that does the work of all the others.

Forces on one line just add. These two are at right angles, so adding their sizes would overstate the result. Instead, treat the two pulls as the sides of a right-angled triangle. The resultant is the long side. If Rx is the pull across and Ry the pull up, Pythagoras gives R = √(Rx² + Ry²). For our post the squares add up to 64 + 225 = 289, and the square root of 289 is 17 kN.

afterFigure.text: Notice that 17 kN is less than 8 + 15 = 23 kN. Two pulls at right angles partly pull in different directions, so they never team up as well as two pulls along one line. This is the same triangle we used to split a force, read in the other direction.

lead.text: The two pulls meet at right angles, so treat them as the sides of a triangle.

Back at the post, suppose we want it to stay perfectly still. Then the ropes must cancel each other out, so that their resultant is zero. A body in that state is in equilibrium. Engineers write the condition as ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0, where Σ (sigma) means “the sum of”: the across pieces add to zero and the up pieces add to zero.

To check, they first draw the post on its own, with every force that acts on it as an arrow and nothing else. No ground, no tree, no people, only arrows. This sketch is called a free-body diagram. Only forces acting on the body belong on it. The post pulls on the rope too, but that force acts on the rope, so it stays off the post's drawing.

afterFigure.text: Drawn tip to tail, the arrows of a body in equilibrium close up into a shape with no gap, because the last arrow ends exactly where the first began. That gives a quick way to find a missing force. Add up the ones you know, and the missing force has the same size as their resultant and points the opposite way.

blocks.text: Picture a strong post in the corner of a yard with a rope tied to its top. One person pulls on the rope and the post leans a little. A second person joins in on the same rope and it leans further. Nothing surprising yet, since two pulls the same way make a bigger pull.

Now a third person takes a second rope and pulls from the side. Someone else runs a rope from the top of the post down to a ring in the ground, so it slants. Each rope pulls in its own direction, and the post feels all of them at once. Bridges, cranes and roof frames face the same situation, with cables and bars pulling at every angle.

This lesson follows the post as the ropes pile on. We start with two pulls along a line and then tilt one, which leads to splitting a slanted pull into two straight ones. After that, pulls at right angles go back together, and the last job is finding the rope that would hold the post perfectly still.

lessons.title: Turning effect: moments

lead.text: Put a spanner on a stuck bolt and push on the end of the handle, at right angles to it. The bolt turns more easily when you push harder, and it turns more easily when the handle is longer. Engineers call the turning effect of a force about a point a moment. The point it turns about is the pivot, which here is the centre of the bolt.

A moment is found by multiplying the force by the distance from the pivot, measured at right angles to the push: M = F × d. With the force in newtons and the distance in metres, the moment comes out in newton-metres (N·m). A 100 N push 0.2 m from the bolt gives 20 N·m, and the same push 0.4 m from the bolt gives 40 N·m. Doubling the distance doubles the moment. Both cases are in the picture below.

afterFigure.text: Moments can turn either way, so they carry a sign. Here anticlockwise is positive and clockwise is negative. For a single push the sign hardly matters, but it will once several forces act on the same body. In practice, distance helps as much as force does. To loosen a tight nut with the least effort, push as far from it as you can, at right angles to the handle.

lead.text: Moment is force times distance, so each option below changes one of them.
The push is at right angles to the handle, so the full distance to the bolt counts.

So far the push has been at right angles to the handle. Real pushes are rarely so tidy, and a hand may push the spanner at a slant. As the first lesson showed, the force then has two components: one across the handle and one along it. The part along the handle only shoves the spanner towards the bolt or away from it, and does nothing to turn the bolt. Only the part across the handle turns it.

For a force F at an angle θ to the handle, the turning part is F sin θ. The moment is then M = F sin θ × d, where d is still the full distance from the bolt along the handle. A quick check is the right-angled case. At θ = 90° the sine is 1, and the formula gives F × d again. As the push swings round towards the handle, the moment shrinks.

afterFigure.text: The picture compares a push at right angles with a slanted push of the same size at the same place. The slanted one turns the bolt less, because less of it acts across the handle.

steps.headline: A 90 N push acts at 30° to a spanner, 0.4 m from the bolt. Find the moment about the bolt.

lead.text: Here is the slanted push in full, with the reason for each line.

workedSteps.text: Only the part of the push across the spanner turns it.
Multiply by the full distance along the spanner.

steps.headline: The 150 N push is now at 30° to the spanner, still 0.3 m from the bolt. Find the moment.

lead.text: Compare the answer with the 45 N·m you found for the same push at right angles.

workedSteps.text: Take the part of the push across the spanner.
Multiply that part by the 0.3 m distance, in N·m.

steps.headline: The line the force acts along

lead.text: There is a second way to see the same rule. Draw the line that the force acts along, called its line of action, and measure from the pivot straight across to that line. The shortest distance, at right angles to the line, is the perpendicular distance. That is the d in M = F × d. For a push at right angles to the handle it equals the distance along the handle. For a slanted push it is shorter, which is why the slanted push turns less.

One consequence is worth stating plainly. If the line of action passes through the pivot, the perpendicular distance is zero, and so is the moment, whatever the size of the force. Try to open a door by pushing on its hinge and it will not budge. Engineers use this the other way round. An unknown force is given a line through the point they take moments about, and it drops out of the equation.

lead.text: Sketch the line the force acts along, then find its perpendicular distance from the bolt.

Moments become useful when more than one force acts on a body. Take a see-saw with its pivot in the middle and a child at each end. One child turns it anticlockwise and the other clockwise. If the two moments are equal, they cancel and the see-saw stays level. Engineers call this equilibrium, as in the first lesson. The moments about the pivot add up to zero, with anticlockwise positive and clockwise negative.

The simplest balanced case has two children at equal distances from the pivot. The distances are equal, so the moments can only be equal if the forces are, which means the children weigh the same. A child's weight is a force, the pull of gravity, acting downwards at the seat.
Think about what must be equal for the two moments to cancel.

Now bring one child closer to the pivot. A heavy child sitting near the middle can balance a lighter child sitting far out, because the shorter distance makes up for the greater weight. Balance still means equal moments: the weight times the distance on one side equals the weight times the distance on the other.

A 200 N child 1.5 m from the pivot has a moment of 300 N·m. A 300 N child 1 m on the other side also has 300 N·m, so the see-saw balances. The picture shows that pair, and what happens when the heavier child moves out to the same distance as the lighter one.

afterFigure.text: This is the working rule for the rest of the course. Write down the moment of each force about the pivot, with its sign, add them up and set the total to zero. Whatever is unknown can then be found.

lead.text: The 300 N child stays where they are, and the heavier child can sit anywhere on the other side.

blocks.text: A wheel nut is stuck fast. You fit a short spanner and push with all your weight, and nothing moves. You swap it for a long wrench and the nut gives. You pushed no harder than before, yet the long handle did what the short one could not.

That everyday experience is the basis for much of engineering. It explains why a crane with a long arm needs a heavy block at the back and why a door handle sits as far from the hinges as it can. In every case a force acts at a distance from a point, and the distance matters as much as the force.
This lesson starts with the stuck nut and works out what decides how hard a push turns it. We then tilt the push, aim it at the nut itself, and finish by using the same idea to balance a see-saw.

lessons.title: Reactions of a supported beam

lead.text: A beam resting on two supports does not fall because each support pushes back up on it. That upward push is called a reaction. The beam presses down on each support with the load it passes on, and by Newton's third law the support presses up with the same force. Reactions are forces we do not know in advance, and finding them is the first job in analysing any structure, since you cannot size a post until you know how much it has to carry.

The beam is at rest, so the forces on it balance. The upward reactions must add up to the downward load. With a 20 kN crate on the plank, the two reactions together make 20 kN. If the crate sits halfway along, nothing favours either support and each carries 10 kN. Slide the crate towards one end and the nearer support will carry more. The rest of this lesson works out by how much.
The crate is at the middle, so nothing favours either support.

The two supports of a beam are rarely the same kind. A pin holds the beam in place. It can push in any direction, but the beam is still free to turn about it. A roller sits on a surface like a wheel on a rail, and it can only push at right angles to that surface, which for a level beam means straight up. The beam is free to slide along a roller and to turn on it.

Engineers usually rest one end of a beam on a pin and the other on a roller. That lets the beam grow and shrink with the temperature without cracking its supports. A third kind, the fixed support, grips the beam so tightly that it cannot turn either, and it appears in a later lesson.

afterFigure.text: With only vertical loads, the pin pushes straight up too, so both supports push up. The picture shows what each kind of support can push with and how the beam may still move.

lead.text: Now put the load nearer one end, and call the left support A and the right support B. The beam is at rest, so the moments about any point must cancel as well as the forces, as the last lesson showed. The trick is to choose the point carefully. Take moments about the support at A. The reaction at A acts through A itself, so its distance from A is zero and it has no moment about A. That leaves the moment of the load and the moment of the reaction at B, which is the only unknown.

Let the beam be 8 m between supports, carrying 16 kN at 3 m from A. About A the load turns the beam one way with a moment of 16 × 3 = 48 kN·m. The reaction at B, written RB, turns it the other way with a moment of RB × 8. Balance needs 8 × RB = 48, so RB = 6 kN. The load is 16 kN in all, so the reaction at A is 16 − 6 = 10 kN.

afterFigure.text: The support nearer the load carries more, which gives a useful check on any answer. The two reactions add up to the load, and the bigger one belongs to the closer support.

lead.text: Take moments about A, so that the reaction at A drops out of the equation.

steps.headline: A load spread along the beam

lead.text: Not every load sits at one point. Sand heaped along a plank, or the weight of a floor, is spread along the beam and described by an intensity such as 2 kN/m, meaning 2 kN on every metre. A load of w kN/m over a length L has a total of w × L. At 2 kN/m over 5 m that is 10 kN.

For finding reactions, the whole spread load can be replaced by one force equal to its total, acting at the middle of the loaded length. For the 10 kN above, starting at the left support, the force acts 2.5 m along. The replacement has the same total and the same moment about any point as the spread load, so it gives the same reactions. The picture compares the two.

afterFigure.text: The shortcut applies to reactions only. Inside the beam, the bending depends on how the load is really spread, and a later lesson looks at that.

lead.text: Use the total of the load and the middle of its length.
Replace the spread load by one force first, then take moments about the left support.

Beams often stick out past a support, like a balcony or a diving board. A load out on the overhang can swing the beam about the nearer support and lift the far end, so the far support has to hold the beam down.

Count upward reactions as positive and keep the sign. Take a beam with supports at x = 0 and x = 6 m and a 9 kN load at the free end, x = 8 m. Moments about x = 0 give 6 × RB = 9 × 8, so RB = 12 kN upward. The reactions must still add up to the load, so RA + 12 = 9 and RA = −3 kN. The minus sign says the reaction at x = 0 points down. A support that could only push would let that end of the beam lift off.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows an overhanging load next to a load between the supports. A negative reaction is the sign that a load has gone beyond a support.

lead.text: Count upward as positive and keep the sign in your answer.

blocks.text: A plank is laid across a stream and rests on a bank at each end. Stand in the middle and it sags a little but holds. Walk towards one bank and the end by that bank takes more of your weight, while the far end takes less. Nobody can see that happening, yet each bank is working harder or less hard as you move.

Floor beams, bridge girders and shelves are the same arrangement. Whoever designs one has to know how much each support must carry, because that decides how strong the posts and walls under it have to be. The answer comes from the turning effects of the last lesson, and it needs no more than a little arithmetic.
This lesson follows a load as it moves along a beam. A crate starts in the middle and slides towards one end. Later the load is spread along the plank, and last of all it hangs past the end.

lessons.title: Trusses: the method of joints

lead.text: A truss is a frame built from straight bars called members, joined at their ends by pins called joints. Loads are applied at the joints and nowhere else. The simplest truss is a single triangle. The load hangs from the top joint, which is called the apex. The two lower corners rest on supports.

A triangle is the building block because it cannot change shape unless a member gets longer or shorter. Push on the corner of a four-sided frame and it folds flat. Push on the corner of a triangle and the members simply resist. Bigger trusses are triangles added to triangles. The picture shows two small ones, each with a 20 kN load at the apex.

afterFigure.text: Because each member is so simple, a truss can carry a large load with very little material. The next screen looks at what each member feels.

lead.text: The load hangs from the middle, so nothing favours either foot.

The members are straight, joined by pins and loaded only at the joints, so each member is acted on only at its two ends. For the member to stay at rest, those two forces must be equal and opposite along its own line. Every member is simply pulled or pushed along its length. A member that is pulled, stretched like a rope, is in tension. A member that is pushed, squashed like a post, is in compression.

Hang a lamp from a rope and the rope is in tension. Stand a post under a floor and the post is in compression. Which one a member is depends on how it acts on the joints at its ends. If it pulls them towards each other it is in tension, and if it pushes them apart it is in compression. The difference matters because a long thin bar copes well with a pull and buckles under a push.

diagram.alt: One straight bar between two joints. In the first view the arrows on the joints point towards each other, which is tension. In the second the arrows point away from each other, which is compression.

lead.text: Picture the rope and ask whether it is being stretched or squashed.

To find the force in a member, imagine cutting the frame apart at one joint and drawing that joint alone with every force on it, as in a free-body diagram. Start at the apex, since only three things act there: the load pulling down and the two sloping members. The truss is symmetrical, so the two sloping members carry equal forces, F.

From the first lesson, a member's upward share is its force times rise ÷ length. Take a truss with a span of 8 m and an apex 3 m high, so that each sloping member is 5 m long. A 30 kN load hangs from the apex. The two members together must hold up the load, so 2 × F × 3/5 = 30, which gives F = 25 kN.

afterFigure.text: That is more than the 15 kN half of the load, because a sloping member only gives 3/5 of its force upwards. The flatter the truss, the harder each sloping member works.

lead.text: Cut out the apex joint. Two equal members meet there and hold up the load between them.

steps.headline: A truss spans 6 m with its apex 4 m high, so each sloping member is 5 m long. A 24 kN load hangs at the apex. Find the force in each sloping member.

lead.text: Here is the same method on a taller truss, written out line by line.

workedSteps.text: At the apex two members share the load, each with vertical share rise over length.
Solve for F.
The members push down and outward on the feet, so they are in compression. The bottom member pulls the feet together, so it is in tension.

lead.text: That settles the sloping members. Now move to the foot of the truss, joint A on the left support. In the 8 m truss a sloping member presses on it with 25 kN along the slope. Its sideways part is 25 × run ÷ length, which is 25 × 4/5 = 20 kN, directed outward along the ground.

Nothing loads the truss sideways, so the pin at A has no horizontal reaction. The only thing left to hold that foot still is the bottom member, which joins the two feet. It must supply 20 kN along the ground to balance the outward push. The force in the bottom member equals the horizontal part of the sloping member's force.

afterFigure.text: Whether the bottom member pushes or pulls on the foot is a separate question, and it decides whether the member is in tension or compression. The next questions come back to it.

steps.headline: At joint A of the 4 m truss with a 1.5 m high apex, AC pushes with 10 kN along a line with run 2 m and length 2.5 m. Find the force in AB, in kN.

lead.text: The bottom member balances the horizontal part of the push from AC.

workedSteps.text: Nothing loads the truss sideways, so the pin at A has no horizontal reaction.
AB must cancel the horizontal part of AC's push: its share is run over length, 2 ÷ 2.5.
Multiply AC's force by that share, in kN.

lead.text: Think about which way the bottom member must act on the foot to stop the sloping members spreading it.

steps.headline: A joint with nothing hanging from it

lead.text: Some members carry no force at all. Add a short vertical member DC that joins the middle of the bottom bar, joint D, to the apex. Look at joint D alone. Nothing hangs from it. The two bottom members meet at D along one straight, horizontal line. DC leaves it vertically.

Balance the vertical forces at D. The horizontal members have no vertical part, so DC is the only member with one. With no load and no other vertical force, DC's own vertical force must be zero. A member like this is called a zero-force member. It still has a use: hang the load from D instead of the apex and DC carries that load up to the apex.
Joint D has no load on it, and the two members along the bottom lie on one line.

blocks.text: Look up inside a barn roof or along the side of a railway bridge and you will see the same pattern repeated: straight bars joined at their ends to make triangles. Nobody puts a thick beam where thin bars will do, and the triangles are what make that possible. Each bar is only ever pulled or pushed along its own length.

Hang a heavy load from the tip of one triangle and every bar feels something. The two sloping bars press down on the feet and try to spread them apart. The bar along the bottom holds them together. Choosing the right size for each bar depends on knowing the force in it.
This lesson works out those forces for a small triangular frame. It uses the first three lessons: splitting a force into parts, sharing a load between supports and balancing forces.

lessons.title: Stress, strain and stiffness

lead.text: The last lesson ended with a force in each bar of a truss. A force on its own does not say whether a bar will cope. A pull of 24 kN is nothing to a thick steel bar, and it may be more than a thin steel rod can take.

Suppose a rod hangs a 24 kN load and you are unsure it is strong enough. One fix is to hang the load from three identical rods side by side. They share the load equally, so each carries 8 kN, a third of the original. Another fix is to use a single rod three times as fat. Either way, the load has three times as much steel to work with.

What the steel feels depends on the force and on how much material shares it. A rod's cross-section is the shape you would see if you sliced it at right angles to its length, and its area is measured in square millimetres (mm²). Three rods side by side have three times the cross-sectional area of one. The next screen puts force and area into one number.

lead.text: Think about the three rods on the last screen. Two rods share a load in just the same way.

Engineers combine force and area into one number called stress: the force carried by each square millimetre of the cross-section. In symbols σ = F ÷ A, where σ (sigma) is the stress, F is the force and A is the cross-sectional area. Take a rod of 200 mm² that holds the 24 kN load alone. That is 24,000 N ÷ 200 mm² = 120 N/mm².

One newton per square millimetre is called a megapascal (MPa), so that rod is at 120 MPa. Using newtons and square millimetres gives megapascals directly, which is why kilonewtons must be converted to newtons first. Hang the same load from three such rods and each carries 8,000 N on 200 mm², which is only 40 MPa. The picture compares a thin rod with a thick one.

afterFigure.text: Stress decides whether steel gives way, and force alone does not. A rod that is comfortable at 40 MPa may be in trouble at 400 MPa, whatever force produced it. The same force on twice the area gives half the stress, which is why a thick bar is safer than a thin one.

lead.text: Convert the load to newtons first, then divide by the area in mm².

Stress describes what the steel is asked to carry. Next comes what the rod does in response. It stretches. A pulled rod gets a little longer, and how much longer depends on how long it was to begin with. A 4 m rod stretches twice as much as a 2 m rod of the same steel under the same stress. So stretch is best measured as a fraction of the original length.

That fraction is called strain, written ε (epsilon). It is the extension δ (delta), the amount the rod lengthens, divided by the original length L: ε = δ ÷ L. Take a rod 5 m long, which is 5,000 mm, that stretches by 4 mm. Its strain is 4 ÷ 5,000 = 0.0008. Strain is a ratio of two lengths, so it has no unit, and both lengths must be in the same unit before you divide.

Stress and strain are linked. While the stress stays low enough for the rod to spring back when released, the strain is proportional to the stress. Double the stress and the strain doubles. The ratio between them belongs to the material and is called Young's modulus, written E. So stress = E × strain, or strain = stress ÷ E.

E measures stiffness: how much stress it takes to produce a given stretch. Structural steel has an E of about 200 GPa. Aluminium alloys have about 70 GPa, so under the same stress an aluminium bar stretches nearly three times as much as a steel bar of the same length. The picture shows the two side by side.

afterFigure.text: Put E in the same unit as the stress before dividing. 1 GPa is 1,000 MPa, so steel is 200,000 MPa. A steel bar at 80 MPa has a strain of 80 ÷ 200,000 = 0.0004. E says how much a bar stretches. How much stress it can survive is a separate property, covered at the end of the lesson.

steps.headline: A 3,000 mm steel bar (E = 200 GPa) carries a stress of 60 MPa. How far does it stretch?

lead.text: Here is the whole method, from the stress to the stretch.

workedSteps.text: Write E in MPa so that it matches the unit of stress.
Strain is stress divided by E.
Stretch is strain times the original length.

steps.headline: The bar is 2,000 mm long and its steel has E = 200 GPa. At 50 MPa, how far does it stretch?

lead.text: The method is the same as in the worked example.

workedSteps.text: Write E in MPa.
Strain is stress divided by E.
Multiply the strain by the original length, in mm.

lead.text: Same method, different material. Aluminium is less stiff than steel.

So far every bar has sprung back to its original length when the load was removed. That holds only up to a limit. Plot stress against strain for a steel bar and the line is straight at first, at a slope of E. Where the straight part ends is the yield stress. Beyond it the bar stretches a lot for a small rise in stress, and when the load is taken off it does not return all the way. It keeps a permanent stretch, called permanent set.

Keep pulling and the stress rises further, up to the ultimate strength, the highest stress the bar can hold. After that the bar thins at one spot and breaks. A stronger steel might have a yield stress of 355 MPa and an ultimate strength of 510 MPa. The picture loads such a bar to two levels, one below its yield stress and one above it.

afterFigure.text: Designers keep working stress well below the yield stress, so that the structure springs back every time the load is removed. The next lesson asks how far below.

lead.text: Compare the load with both strengths before you decide.

blocks.text: Stretch a rubber band and you can see it get longer. A steel rod does the same, by an amount too small for the eye to notice. A 2 m steel tie pulled hard may lengthen by only a millimetre or so. A designer still needs to know how much, and whether the tie will return to its old length when the load is removed.

The last lesson gave the force in each bar of a truss. A force of 40 kN is nothing to a thick steel bar and is ruinous to a thin wire. The force alone does not say whether a bar is safe, and it does not say how far the bar will stretch either. Something else has to be measured first.
This lesson follows one steel rod as the load on it grows. We first work out how hard the steel is working, then how far it stretches, and finish at the load where it stops springing back.

intro.promise: By the end you'll turn a load into a stress, and a stress into a stretch.

recap.keyIdea: Stress is force over area, and in the elastic range it is E times the strain. Past yield, a bar keeps a permanent stretch.

blocks.text: Back at the hanging rod, you turned a 20 kN pull on 400 mm² into 50 MPa, and found that it stretches a 2,000 mm steel bar by 0.5 mm. The same stress stretches a 1,400 mm aluminium bar by 1 mm, because aluminium is less stiff.

recap.nextHook: A real design never runs a bar at its limit, and the next lesson works out how much margin to leave below the yield stress.

lessons.title: Factor of safety and sizing

steps.headline: Working stress and the factor of safety

lead.text: A tie is a bar that is pulled along its length, like the bottom chord of a truss. Last lesson you found the stress in such a bar, the force on each square millimetre of its cross-section. The stress it actually carries in use is its working stress, and the bar stays safe only while that is below the yield stress, the point where it stops springing back.

How far below is found by dividing one by the other. The factor of safety is the yield stress divided by the working stress. Take a tie of 200 mm² that carries 24 kN, in steel that yields at 360 MPa. Its working stress is 24,000 N ÷ 200 mm² = 120 MPa, so its factor of safety is 360 ÷ 120 = 3. The tie could take three times its working stress before it began to yield. The picture shows the same tie at two loads.

afterFigure.text: At 48 kN the same tie works at 240 MPa and the factor falls to 1.5. Doubling the load halves the factor, and a bar loaded right up to its yield stress has a factor of exactly 1.
The same ratio works with loads. For one bar, the load that would make it yield divided by the load it carries gives the same number, because the area cancels.

lead.text: Compare what the cable can take with what it is asked to take. The ratio from the last screen works on loads as well as stresses.
Find the working stress in MPa first, then compare it with the yield stress.

Once you can measure a margin, you have to decide how big it should be. The factor of safety covers everything that might make a bar weaker, or its load heavier, than the designer allowed for. A crowd or a gust of wind can arrive on top of the expected load. The steel can be a little weaker than its datasheet says, or lose some thickness to rust. The calculation itself can hold a mistake nobody has found.

The size of the margin follows from how well those things are known and what happens if they go wrong. Where the loads are known closely and weight matters a great deal, as in an aircraft, factors near 1.5 are used. Building frames use somewhat more, often around 2. A lift cable or a crane hook carries people or hangs over them, so it gets a much larger factor, because a failure there costs lives.
Whatever the factor, the designer fixes it first and lets it decide the size of the bar. The next screen shows how.

Turn the formula round. When the factor of safety is chosen in advance, the highest working stress you will permit is the yield stress divided by it. This is the allowable stress. Steel that yields at 300 MPa, used with a factor of 2, has an allowable stress of 300 ÷ 2 = 150 MPa.

The allowable stress answers two kinds of question. If you know the area, the largest load is the allowable stress times the area. A bar of 200 mm² can carry 150 N/mm² × 200 mm² = 30,000 N, which is 30 kN. If you know the load, the smallest area is the load divided by the allowable stress. A 42 kN load needs 42,000 N ÷ 150 N/mm² = 280 mm².
Keep the load in newtons and the stress in MPa and the area comes out in mm² with no further conversion.

steps.headline: A tie must carry 30 kN with a factor of safety of 2. The steel yields at 250 MPa. Find the least area.

lead.text: Here is the method from the last screen, written out line by line.

workedSteps.text: Divide the yield stress by the factor to get the allowable stress.
Area is the load in newtons over the allowable stress.

steps.headline: A tie must carry 60 kN with a factor of safety of 2, using steel that yields at 250 MPa. Find the least area.

lead.text: The method is the same as in the worked example.

workedSteps.text: Divide the yield stress by the factor to get the allowable stress.
Divide the load in newtons by the allowable stress, to get the area in mm².

lead.text: The area you calculate is a minimum, and mills do not make a bar of every size. A designer picks from a list, such as square bars with sides of 12 mm and 16 mm. The area of a square bar is its side squared, so these have 144 mm² and 256 mm².

Suppose a calculation asks for at least 200 mm², for a load of 25 kN at an allowable stress of 125 MPa. The 12 mm bar is too small. It would work at 25,000 ÷ 144, about 174 MPa, which is above the 125 MPa allowed. The 16 mm bar works at about 98 MPa, so it is the smallest bar that passes. The picture shows both.

afterFigure.text: Rounding up leaves a factor of safety a little above the one you chose, which is the safe direction. Rounding down never is, so you take the smallest bar whose area is at least what the calculation gave.

lead.text: Work out the area of each bar in turn and drop any that is too small. Then take the smallest one left.

steps.headline: Strong enough is not always stiff enough

lead.text: A bar can pass every strength check and still be a poor tie, because it also stretches. If the tie holds something that must stay in line, the stretch can matter as much as the strength. You found the stretch of a loaded bar last lesson: strain is the stress divided by E, and the stretch is the strain times the original length.

Take a steel tie of 400 mm² and 4 m length, carrying 30 kN. Its stress is 30,000 ÷ 400 = 75 MPa. With E = 200,000 MPa the strain is 75 ÷ 200,000 = 0.000375, and over 4,000 mm that is a stretch of 0.000375 × 4,000 = 1.5 mm.

Whether 1.5 mm is acceptable depends on the job. A roof tie can usually take it, and a rod that holds a machine in line cannot. When the stretch sets the limit, the bar is chosen to meet it, and the factor of safety ends up higher than the design needed.
The tie in this question passes the strength check. This time the question is how far it stretches. Use E = 200,000 MPa.

lessons.orientation: Size a member for strength with a margin, then check that it is stiff enough.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: The last lesson followed a steel rod as its load grew, up to the stress where it stops springing back. Nobody loads a bar that far on purpose. A lift cable can carry a load many times heavier than any lift will put on it, and the bolts in a bridge and the chain on a crane hook are chosen the same way.

That spare strength is deliberate, and it has a price, because a stronger part is thicker, heavier and dearer. With too little spare strength, one bad day brings the structure down. With too much, the design wastes material or becomes too heavy to lift into place.

This lesson follows one steel tie, a bar that is pulled along its length. We measure how much spare strength it has and decide how much it should have. That choice sets the size of the tie, and a last check shows whether a bar strong enough also stretches too far.

intro.promise: By the end you'll size a steel member from a factor of safety, and check that it does not stretch too much.

recap.keyIdea: The factor of safety is the yield stress divided by the working stress. To size a member, divide the yield stress by the factor to get the allowable stress, then find the area and check the stretch.

blocks.text: The cable that holds five times its load has a factor of safety of 5. For the steel tie you found a factor of 2.5 at 40 kN on 400 mm². You then sized a tie for 60 kN at a factor of 2, which needed 480 mm² and so the 25 mm square bar. That bar stretches 1.44 mm over 3 m, so strength and stiffness are separate checks.

recap.nextHook: Every bar so far was pulled straight along its length. A beam carries loads across it, and the next lesson cuts one in half to see what holds each piece in place.

lessons.title: Shear force and bending moment

lead.text: Suppose you saw the plank in two, 2 m from the left end, and somehow keep both pieces exactly where they were. Before the cut the left piece was at rest, and it stays at rest, so the forces on it must still balance. The left post pushes up on it with 9 kN. The crate is further along, on the other piece. Nothing else pushes down on the left piece, so the cut face must supply a 9 kN downward force.
That force across the cut is the shear force, written V. Its size equals the sum of the vertical forces on the left piece, and we count upward forces as positive, so here V = +9 kN.

You could keep the right piece instead. The 15 kN crate pulls it down and the 6 kN post pushes it up, which leaves 9 kN downward that the cut face must hold up. The answer has the same size, and it acts the other way, as the two faces of a cut should.
Cut the plank, keep the left piece, and ask what must act on it for it to stay at rest.

steps.headline: How the shear changes along the plank

lead.text: Slide the cut along the 10 m plank and the shear force follows it. For any cut between the left end and the crate, the left piece holds only the left post's 9 kN, so V is +9 kN along that whole stretch. Move the cut past the crate and the 15 kN crate joins the left piece, pulling it down. Now V = 9 − 15 = −6 kN. The picture plots the shear along the plank.

afterFigure.text: The shear jumps at the crate by the crate's own 15 kN and then stays at −6 kN to the right-hand end. The minus sign says that the net force on the left piece now points downward, and its size, 6 kN, matches the right post's push. That has to be so, because that post alone is left to hold up the right-hand piece.

lead.text: The load sits at x = 2 m. Cut just to the right of it, so that the left reaction and the load are both on the left piece.

Shear is only half of what a cut face does. The left piece has a post pushing up at one end and a cut at the other, and a push at a distance twists a piece, as a spanner twists a nut. For the piece not to turn, the cut face must also supply a turning effect. That is the bending moment, written M. It is the total moment of all the forces on the piece, taken about the cut.

On the 10 m plank, cut under the crate, 4 m from the left end. The left piece has one force on it, the post's 9 kN, acting 4 m from the cut, so M = 9 × 4 = 36 kN·m. A cut 2 m from the left end gives 9 × 2 = 18 kN·m. A moment that bends a beam into a smile, hollow side up, is called sagging and counts as positive. The forces on the right piece give the same moment, so use whichever piece has fewer forces.
A moment is a force times its distance from the point you take moments about.

steps.headline: A 6 m beam on end supports carries 15 kN at x = 4 m. Find the bending moment under the load.

lead.text: Here is the whole method, line by line.

workedSteps.text: Find the left reaction with moments about B.
Cut under the load. Only RA is to its left, 4 m away.

steps.headline: On the 6 m beam, the 12 kN crate is at x = 2 m and the left reaction is 8 kN. Find the bending moment under the crate.

lead.text: The method is the same as in the worked example.

workedSteps.text: Cut just under the crate. Only the left reaction is on the left piece.
It acts 2 m from the cut. Multiply, in kN·m.

steps.headline: A load spread along the beam

lead.text: Not every load sits at a point. A floor or a layer of snow spreads its weight along the beam, and engineers give it in kilonewtons per metre, kN/m. A uniform load of w kN/m over a span of L metres weighs w × L in all. For finding moments it can be treated as that single weight, acting at the middle of the stretch it covers. The picture shows a beam carrying 2 kN/m over 6 m, and the same weight gathered at midspan.

afterFigure.text: That load weighs 2 × 6 = 12 kN, so each post holds up 6 kN. Cut at midspan, 3 m from the left end. The left piece has the post's 6 kN pushing up 3 m from the cut. It also carries half of the spread load, 2 × 3 = 6 kN, pulling down with its centre 1.5 m from the cut. So M = 6 × 3 − 6 × 1.5 = 18 − 9 = 9 kN·m.

Done in symbols for any uniform load, the same steps give M = wL² ÷ 8, which here is 2 × 36 ÷ 8 = 9 kN·m. By symmetry, midspan is where this beam is bent most. Gathering the same weight at midspan, the second case in the picture, bends it more, because none of the weight is spread towards the posts.

lead.text: The largest moment is at midspan. Use the result from the last screen, or balance the left half of the beam yourself.

steps.headline: A single load, and a cantilever

lead.text: A single load gives a simpler answer. Put a load P at the middle of a beam of span L. By symmetry each post carries P ÷ 2. Cut under the load and the left piece has P ÷ 2 acting L ÷ 2 from the cut, so M = P ÷ 2 × L ÷ 2 = PL ÷ 4. For a 6 m beam with a 12 kN load at midspan that is 12 × 6 ÷ 4 = 18 kN·m.

A cantilever is a beam held by a wall at one end and free at the other. Cut it next to the wall and look at the free piece, which has only the load acting on it. The moment is then the load times its distance from the wall, so a 4 m cantilever with 6 kN at its tip has M = 6 × 4 = 24 kN·m at the wall. It bends the other way from a plank, hollow side down. That is called hogging, and a hogging moment counts as negative.

steps.headline: Shear is the slope of the moment

lead.text: Go along the 10 m plank from the left end and watch the moment. It starts at zero, because no force lies to the left of a cut at the very end. Each metre you move the cut to the right adds the shear to the moment, so the moment rises by 9 kN·m per metre while the shear is +9 kN. That is the general rule: the slope of the moment curve at any point equals the shear force there. The picture shows the moment and the shear of the plank side by side.

afterFigure.text: After the crate the shear is −6 kN, so the moment falls by 6 kN·m per metre. It comes down from 36 kN·m at the crate to zero at the right-hand end, as it must at a post with nothing beyond it. The moment curve is highest where it stops climbing and begins to fall.

lead.text: Look at the top of the moment curve on the last screen, and use the slope rule on what is happening there.

lessons.orientation: Cut a beam, balance one piece and draw how shear and moment vary along it.

blocks.text: A plank 10 m long rests on a post at each end. A crate of 15 kN sits on it, 4 m from the left end. From the earlier lessons you know what the posts do. The left post pushes up with 9 kN and the right post with 6 kN, and the plank stays put because those two pushes balance the crate.

That tells you what happens at the ends and nothing about what goes on inside the wood. At every point along the plank one side is pulling or pushing on the other, and some places work much harder than others. A plank that snaps does so at one particular place, and an engineer needs to know which.

This lesson saws the plank in two, in the imagination, and asks what the cut face must do to keep each piece where it was. That gives two quantities at every point along a beam, one for sliding and one for turning. Together they show where the beam is most at risk.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the shear force and bending moment at any cut along a beam, and say where the moment peaks.

recap.keyIdea: At any cut, the shear force is the sum of the vertical forces on one piece and the bending moment is their total moment about the cut. The moment peaks where the shear passes through zero.

blocks.text: Back at the plank, the cut at 2 m carried a shear of 9 kN, and the cut under the crate carried a moment of 36 kN·m, the largest anywhere on it. On the shorter beam you found a shear of −4 kN just beyond a 12 kN load and 16 kN·m under it. A uniform 3 kN/m over 8 m peaks at 24 kN·m, at midspan, where the shear passes through zero.

recap.nextHook: The bending moment squeezes one face of a beam and stretches the other. The next lesson works out how hard the material is working at those faces.

lessons.title: Bending stress and the I-beam

lead.text: Bend a ruler between your hands and look at its two faces. The face on the outside of the curve gets longer, so that layer of material is stretched. The face on the inside gets shorter, so it is squeezed. Between them there is a layer that keeps its length. The line where it crosses the cross-section is the neutral axis, and in a shape that is the same above and below, like a rectangle, it runs along the middle.

Layers further from the neutral axis stretch or shorten by more, in proportion to their distance from it. We call that distance y, and engineers call each thin layer a fibre. Strain grows with y, and stress is E times strain, so the stress grows with y as well. It is zero at the neutral axis and largest at the outer fibre, the fibre furthest from the axis.
Use what you have just read about where the neutral axis sits in a symmetric section.

Now the stress needs a number. At a distance y from the neutral axis, σ = M × y ÷ I. Here M is the bending moment and I is a property of the cross-section called the second moment of area. A bigger moment or a larger y gives a bigger stress, and a larger I gives a smaller one.

I measures how well the shape of a section resists bending. It is not the area. It counts each bit of area more heavily the further it sits from the neutral axis, so material far out helps a great deal and material near the axis hardly helps. Its unit is mm⁴, because it comes from an area times a distance squared. To get the stress in MPa, turn kN·m into N·mm by multiplying by 10⁶ and use mm for y and mm⁴ for I.

steps.headline: The second moment of a rectangle

lead.text: For a rectangle of width b and depth h, the second moment of area about its neutral axis is I = b × h³ ÷ 12. The depth h is the size measured in the direction of the bending, from the squeezed face to the stretched one. It is cubed, and the width is not. A beam 120 mm wide and 100 mm deep has I = 120 × 100³ ÷ 12 = 10 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

afterFigure.text: Put a moment of 4 kN·m on it, which is 4 × 10⁶ N·mm. The outer fibre is half the depth from the axis, so y = 50 mm and σ = 4 × 10⁶ × 50 ÷ (10 × 10⁶) = 20 MPa. The picture shows this section, and the same section turned to stand 100 mm wide and 120 mm deep.

lead.text: Compare the two orientations of the section on the last screen, and think about what the depth does in the formula.
Work in newtons and millimetres, where 1 kN·m is 10⁶ N·mm. The largest stress is at the outer fibre.

steps.headline: A beam 50 mm wide and 120 mm deep carries 6 kN·m. Find the largest bending stress.

lead.text: Here is the whole method, line by line.

workedSteps.text: Find I for the rectangle.
The largest stress is at the outer fibre, half the depth from the axis.
Put the moment in N·mm and use σ = My/I.

steps.headline: The same plank is laid flat, 200 mm wide and 100 mm deep, under the same 20 kN·m. Find the largest bending stress.

lead.text: The method is the same as in the worked example.

workedSteps.text: Swap the width and depth in bh³/12.
The outer fibre is now half of 100 mm from the axis.
Use σ = My/I, with M in N·mm, to get the stress in MPa.

lead.text: Compare the two answers for the plank. On its edge, 200 mm deep, the largest stress was 30 MPa. Laid flat, 100 mm deep, it was 60 MPa. Halving the depth cut I to an eighth, and doubling the width brought it back up to a quarter. Meanwhile y halved. A quarter of the I with half the distance leaves twice the stress.

The cube in bh³ ÷ 12 is what makes depth so powerful. Suppose a beam keeps its width and its depth is tripled. I grows by 3³ = 27 times while y only triples, so for the same moment the stress falls to a ninth. Making a beam deeper is a cheap way to make it strong, which is why floor joists stand on edge and why a steel beam is deeper than it is wide.
Cube the depth before you multiply by the width.

The stress is small near the neutral axis, so wood or steel there does little work, yet it still adds weight. A steel I-section puts most of its metal in two wide flanges at the top and bottom, where the stress is greatest. A thin web along the middle joins them. The beam keeps much of the stiffness of a solid one with a fraction of the metal. The picture compares an I-section with a solid rectangle of the same outline.

afterFigure.text: To find I for an I-section, take the outer rectangle and subtract the two empty regions beside the web. Take a section 80 mm wide and 150 mm deep, with 10 mm flanges and an 8 mm web. Each empty region is (80 − 8) ÷ 2 = 36 mm wide and 150 − 20 = 130 mm deep, so I = (80 × 150³ − 72 × 130³) ÷ 12 = 9.32 × 10⁶ mm⁴. The solid 80 × 150 rectangle has 22.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴, so the I-section keeps 41 percent of the stiffness with 22 percent of the area.

lead.text: Find I as the outer rectangle minus the two empty side regions, as on the last screen.

lessons.orientation: Use σ = My/I and see why depth and flanges make a beam efficient.

blocks.text: Take a 100 mm by 200 mm plank from a timber yard and lay it across a gap to make a small bridge. Stand on the middle and it bends a little. Now turn it on to its narrow edge and stand on it again. Wood, span and weight are all the same, yet the plank behaves differently.

The last lesson gave the bending moment at every point along a beam. That says how hard the beam is being bent. It does not yet say how hard the wood is working, and two planks under the same moment can be working very differently depending on the way up they sit and the shape of their cross-section.

This lesson follows the stress through the depth of a beam, from the squeezed face to the stretched one. It ends with a formula that turns a bending moment into a stress, and with a reason why steel beams are shaped like the letter I.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the largest bending stress in a beam, and see why deep sections and I-beams carry bending well.

recap.keyIdea: Bending stress is σ = My/I, zero at the neutral axis and largest at the outer fibre. For a rectangle I = bh³/12, so depth matters far more than width.

blocks.text: Back at the plank, you found 30 MPa standing on edge and 60 MPa laid flat under the same 20 kN·m. You also found that a 200 mm deep I-section keeps about 31 percent of the solid rectangle's I with about 15 percent of its material.

recap.nextHook: A beam that is strong enough can still sag, and a floor that bounces is a failure of another kind. The next lesson works out how far a beam sags and what controls it.

lessons.title: Deflection and stiffness

lead.text: The simplest beam to study is the cantilever, a bar fixed at one end and free at the other. Hang a load P on the free end, which is the tip. The tip moves down by an amount called the tip deflection, written δ. While the steel stays elastic, springing back when the load is removed, the deflection is proportional to the load, just as the stretch of a rod is proportional to its force.

So a bracket that sags 4 mm under 2 kN sags 8 mm under 4 kN and 2 mm under 1 kN. That gives a quick way to scale a result: find how far it moves under one load and every other load follows by proportion. The rule fails only when the load is big enough to push the steel past its yield stress, which is a different problem.
The cantilever stays within its elastic range, so everything on the last screen applies.

Load is only one thing that sets the deflection. For a cantilever of length L with a load P at the tip, δ = P × L³ ÷ (3 × E × I). The load is on top, as we expected. So is the length, and it is cubed. Triple the length and the tip drops 27 times as far, because a longer bar gives the load a longer lever and also has more bar to bend. The picture shows the same bar at two lengths.

afterFigure.text: E is Young's modulus, the measure of how strongly the material resists stretching, and I is the second moment of area, the shape factor from the last lesson. They sit together underneath, and their product EI is called the flexural rigidity. Double either one and the deflection halves. Steel has E = 200 GPa and aluminium about 70 GPa, so an aluminium arm of the same size sags nearly three times as far.

lead.text: Keep the load and the section the same and change only the length.

The formula works only when every quantity is in a consistent set of units. Use newtons for P, metres for L, pascals for E and metres to the fourth for I. Then δ comes out in metres. The conversions are where mistakes happen. 1 GPa is 10⁹ Pa, so steel's E is 200 × 10⁹ Pa. Since 1 mm is 10⁻³ m, 1 mm⁴ is 10⁻¹² m⁴, which makes 10⁶ mm⁴ equal to 10⁻⁶ m⁴.

Take steel with I = 3 × 10⁶ mm⁴, which is 3 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴. Then EI = 200 × 10⁹ × 3 × 10⁻⁶ = 600,000 N·m². With EI in these units, work out P × L³ in newtons and cubic metres, divide by 3EI, and multiply the answer in metres by 1,000 to get millimetres.
Convert both quantities to base units before you multiply.

steps.headline: A steel cantilever 3 m long (E = 200 GPa, I = 4 × 10⁶ mm⁴) carries 2 kN at its tip. Find the tip deflection.

lead.text: Here is the whole method, line by line.

workedSteps.text: Write E and I in base units.
Work out PL³ in newtons and metres.
Divide by 3EI, then convert to millimetres.

steps.headline: An aluminium cantilever 1 m long (E = 70 GPa, I = 1 × 10⁶ mm⁴) carries 2.1 kN at its tip. Find the tip deflection.

lead.text: The method is the same as in the worked example, with a less stiff metal.

workedSteps.text: Write E and I in base units.
Work out PL³ in newtons and metres.
Divide by 3EI, then convert to millimetres.

steps.headline: Sizing a section for a limit

lead.text: Designers often work the formula backwards. A deflection limit comes with the job: a shelf may be allowed to sag only so far before it looks wrong, and a machine arm far less. With P, L, E and the limit δ known, rearrange the formula to give the section that is needed, I = P × L³ ÷ (3 × E × δ).

Take a steel arm 3 m long that carries 1 kN at its tip and may sag by at most 10 mm. In base units I = 1,000 × 27 ÷ (3 × 200 × 10⁹ × 0.01) = 27,000 ÷ (6 × 10⁹) = 4.5 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴, which is 4.5 × 10⁶ mm⁴. Any section with at least that second moment of area keeps the sag inside the limit.

Sometimes the useful question is how much load it takes to move the tip by a given amount. That is the stiffness, k = P ÷ δ, the load for each unit of deflection, in kN/mm or kN/m. A stiff arm needs a lot of load to move it. A diving board is made with low stiffness so that it gives.

For the cantilever, putting δ = PL³ ÷ 3EI into k = P ÷ δ gives k = 3EI ÷ L³. Stiffness falls with the cube of the length, so halving the length makes an arm eight times as stiff. Take an arm with EI = 600,000 N·m² and L = 2 m. Then k = 3 × 600,000 ÷ 8 = 225,000 N/m, which is 225 kN/m. A load of 0.9 kN moves its tip 0.9 ÷ 225 = 0.004 m, or 4 mm.
Stiffness is the load for each unit of deflection.
A machine-tool arm must hold a cutter steady, so engineers ask how much load it takes to move the tip. Use k = 3EI ÷ L³.

blocks.text: Stand at the end of a diving board and you feel it give. Nothing is damaged, and the board is working well below the stress it can carry, but it bends and the end drops. A shelf that droops under books has the same trouble, and so does a machine arm that wobbles under its cutter.

The last lesson checked that a beam is strong enough. Here the question is how far it moves. A beam can pass every strength check and still be useless if it sags too much, because a door will not shut under a drooping lintel and a cutter cannot hold its line on a bending arm.
We follow one simple beam, a bar fixed at one end with a load on the free end. We find what the sag depends on and put numbers on it. We finish with a measure of how stiff the bar is.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find how far a cantilever sags under load, and say which change stiffens it most.

recap.keyIdea: A cantilever's tip deflection is PL³/3EI: it grows with the cube of the length and shrinks with EI. Stiffness is the load per unit deflection, 3EI/L³.

blocks.text: Back at the board, you found that a 2 m steel cantilever with 3 kN at its tip sags 20 mm, and 160 mm if it is twice as long. Its stiffness is 150 kN/m, and 5 × 10⁶ mm⁴ of I keeps the sag within 8 mm.

recap.nextHook: Beams hold a structure still. Machines use the same forces and distances to do work, and the simplest of them is the spanner that frees a stuck nut.

lessons.title: Levers and pulleys

lead.text: A lever is a rigid bar that turns about a fixed point called the fulcrum. Think of a crowbar prying up a heavy lid. The fulcrum is the point where the bar rests on the ground. Your hand supplies the effort, the force you apply. The lid pushes back with the load, the force you are working against.

You met moments earlier in the course: a force times its distance from the pivot. A lever held at rest has its moments balanced about the fulcrum, so effort × effort arm = load × load arm, where each arm is the distance from the fulcrum to where that force acts. Say the lid pushes back with 600 N at 0.1 m from the fulcrum, and your hand is 0.5 m from it. The moments balance when effort × 0.5 = 600 × 0.1, so the effort is 60 ÷ 0.5 = 120 N.
The spanner works the same way. The nut needs a fixed turning effect, and a longer arm supplies it with less force.
The nut needs the same turning effect whichever spanner you use.

The ratio of the load to the effort tells you how much a lever multiplies your force. It is called mechanical advantage, MA = load ÷ effort. In the prying example the effort is 120 N for a 600 N load, so MA = 600 ÷ 120 = 5. Because effort × effort arm = load × load arm, the same number comes from the arms: MA = effort arm ÷ load arm = 0.5 ÷ 0.1 = 5.

A mechanical advantage above 1 means the lever gives out more force than you put in. It does not give out more energy. The long arm moves through a bigger distance than the short one, and you pay for the extra force with extra distance. The end of this lesson comes back to that cost.
Use the ratio of the arms that you have just met.

steps.headline: A 2 m bar balances an 800 N load 0.25 m from the fulcrum, with the effort at the far end. Find the effort.

lead.text: Here is the whole method, line by line.

workedSteps.text: Moments about the fulcrum balance.
Work out the load's moment, then divide by the effort arm.

steps.headline: The crowbar's handle is 1.2 m from the fulcrum and the 900 N load is 0.2 m from it. Find the effort.

lead.text: The method is the same as in the worked example.

workedSteps.text: Moments about the fulcrum balance.
Divide by the effort arm, in newtons.

lead.text: So far the fulcrum has sat between your hand and the load. That is one of three arrangements, named by which of the three points, fulcrum, load or effort, lies in the middle. Each arrangement is called a lever class.

A first-class lever has the fulcrum in the middle, as on a seesaw or a crowbar. With the load in the middle, as in a nutcracker or a bottle opener, the lever is second class, and its effort arm is longer than its load arm, so the effort is smaller than the load. Put the effort in the middle and the lever is third class. Its effort arm is shorter than its load arm, so the effort has to be larger than the load. That looks like a loss, but it buys speed and reach, because a small movement of the effort gives a large movement of the load. The picture shows one of each.

afterFigure.text: Your forearm is a third-class lever. The elbow is the fulcrum. The biceps pulls a short distance from it, with a weight in your hand at the far end. If the biceps acts at one seventh of the distance from the elbow to the hand, it must pull with seven times the weight you hold. The same moment balance as for the crowbar gives the answer.

lead.text: Find which of the three points sits between the other two.

steps.headline: Pulleys and the block and tackle

lead.text: A pulley is a wheel with a groove for a rope. One fixed pulley only changes the direction of the pull. Mount several pulleys in two blocks, one fixed and one moving with the load. Run one continuous rope through them all. That arrangement is a block and tackle.

Ignoring friction, one rope has the same tension all along it. Each strand that supports the moving block pulls on it with that tension, and the tension is the effort you pull with. The supporting strands share the load, so with n of them, effort = load ÷ n. A 500 N load on 2 strands needs 250 N, and on 5 strands it needs 100 N, so the mechanical advantage is the number of strands. Count only the strands that attach to the moving block or run round it. The picture shows both.
The supporting strands share the load equally.

A lever or pulley that cuts the force must cost something, and the cost is distance. In an ideal machine the work you put in equals the work done on the load. Work is a force times the distance it moves, measured in joules. Take the 5-strand tackle lifting a 500 N load by 0.4 m. The work done on the load is 500 × 0.4 = 200 J.

The effort is 100 N, so for 100 N × distance to make 200 J you must pull 2 m of rope. A direct count agrees. Lifting the block 0.4 m shortens each of the 5 supporting strands by 0.4 m, and all that rope has to come out through your hands: 5 × 0.4 = 2 m. A lever behaves the same way, because the long end swings through a longer arc than the short end. A gain in force is always paid for in distance and never in work.
Every supporting strand gets shorter by the height of the lift, and the rope it gives up passes through your hands.

lessons.orientation: Trade distance for force with levers and rope systems, and count what it costs.

blocks.text: A wheel nut on a car is stuck. A short spanner will not shift it, no matter how hard you push. Someone fetches the long spanner from the boot and the nut comes off with a steady push. You did not get stronger, and the nut did not change.

The first half of this course was about structures that stay still, where forces and moments balance. A spanner works by the same balance with one difference: you choose where to put your hand, and the balance rewards you for choosing well. Machines that multiply a force are built around that idea.

This lesson looks at two of the simplest machines for multiplying a force: a bar that turns about a point, and a rope run over wheels. It finds how much force each needs and sorts the bars into three kinds. It ends with the price you pay for the saving.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the effort a lever or pulley needs for a load, and see what it costs you in distance.

recap.keyIdea: A lever balances effort × effort arm against load × load arm, and a pulley with n strands divides the load by n. Both trade distance for force.

blocks.text: Back at the spanner, a longer arm meant less force for the same turning effect. A crowbar with a 1.2 m handle and a 0.2 m load arm has a mechanical advantage of 6, so it holds 900 N with 150 N. A 4-strand pulley holds 800 N with 200 N, but you pull 2 m of rope to lift the load 0.5 m.

recap.nextHook: Levers and pulleys trade distance for force. Gears do the same job for something that spins, and the next lesson shows how the number of teeth sets the speed.

lessons.title: Gear trains: speed and torque

lead.text: A bicycle's gears are wheels with teeth cut around the rim. Each one is fixed to a shaft, a rod that turns along with it. When two gears mesh, the teeth of one slot between the teeth of the other, so as one turns it pushes the other round. The gear you turn is the driver, and the gear it pushes is the driven gear.

Gear speeds are given in rpm, which stands for revolutions per minute: a gear at 60 rpm turns once every second. The teeth cannot slip, so the two gears must pass teeth at the same rate where they touch. Take a driver with 20 teeth that makes one full turn. Twenty teeth go past the contact point, so twenty teeth of the driven gear go past too. If the driven gear also has 20 teeth, that is a whole turn for it as well. If it has 40 teeth, twenty of them are only half a turn.

afterFigure.text: So the gear with more teeth turns more slowly, and the gear with fewer teeth turns faster. Multiply each gear's speed by its number of teeth and you get the same answer for both: in the second pair, 600 × 20 for the driver and 300 × 40 for the driven gear are both 12,000. Engineers describe a pair by its gear ratio, the driven gear's teeth divided by the driver's teeth. Here that is 40 ÷ 20 = 2, and the driven gear turns at the driver's speed divided by 2.

lead.text: Count the teeth that pass the contact point in one turn of the driver. The figure shows two pairs, and only one of them matches the question.

A pair of gears changes the speed, and it changes how hard the output shaft pushes as well. That needs a word. The turning effect of a force on a shaft is its torque, found like a moment: the force times its distance from the axis. A pedal pushed with 100 N at 0.2 m from the axle gives a torque of 100 × 0.2 = 20 N·m.

The second idea is power, the energy delivered each second. A turning shaft delivers more power the larger its torque and the faster it turns, so doubling either one doubles the power. Now take an ideal mesh, one whose teeth waste no energy. Whatever power goes into the driver comes out of the driven gear, so torque × speed has to be the same on both.

afterFigure.text: That settles the trade. If the driven gear turns at half the speed, its torque must be double. A 20-tooth driver delivering 10 N·m to a 40-tooth gear passes on a shaft that turns at half the speed with 20 N·m. Slow the shaft down by any factor and the torque rises by the same factor. It is the lever bargain again: the lever gave a bigger force over a shorter distance, and a gear pair gives a bigger torque at a lower speed.

lead.text: The mesh keeps the power the same. Decide what must happen to the torque when the speed falls.

steps.headline: A 24-tooth driver turns at 600 rpm and supplies 8 N·m to a 72-tooth gear. The mesh is lossless. Find the output speed and torque.

lead.text: Here is the whole method for a pair of gears, line by line.

workedSteps.text: The gear ratio is driven teeth over driver teeth.
Speed falls by the ratio.
The power is kept, so torque rises by the ratio.

steps.headline: The 20-tooth driver supplies 10 N·m and the mesh is lossless. Find the output torque on the 60-tooth gear.

lead.text: The method is the same as in the worked example.

workedSteps.text: The gear ratio is driven teeth over driver teeth.
Torque rises by the ratio. Multiply the input torque, in N·m.

lead.text: Two gears that mesh push on each other at the contact point, and that reverses the turning. Where the driver's rim moves down, the driven gear's rim moves up, so one turns clockwise while the other turns anticlockwise. Sometimes you want the output to turn the same way as the input. Sometimes the two shafts sit too far apart for the gears to meet.

The fix is a third gear between them, called an idler. It meshes with the driver on one side and with the output gear on the other. The idler turns against the driver, and the output turns against the idler, which sends the output round in the same direction as the driver.

afterFigure.text: The idler's speed follows the usual rule against the driver, and then its tooth count cancels out of the final answer. Take a 24-tooth driver at 600 rpm with a 36-tooth idler and a 48-tooth output. The idler turns at 600 × 24 ÷ 36 = 400 rpm, and the output turns at 400 × 36 ÷ 48 = 300 rpm. Without the idler, 600 × 24 ÷ 48 is also 300 rpm. An idler changes which way the output turns and how far apart the shafts sit. It leaves the speed ratio alone.

lead.text: The idler meshes directly with the driver, so the output gear does not come into this part of the problem.

A bicycle does not mesh its gears directly. The pedals turn a large toothed wheel, the chainring, and a chain carries the motion to a small toothed wheel on the back wheel, the sprocket. The chain's links fit over the teeth of both wheels, so it carries teeth past each of them at the same rate, just as a mesh does. The rule is the same as before: speed × teeth is equal on both.

The direction is different. A chain loops from one wheel to the other and reverses nothing, so both turn the same way. Suppose the chainring has 40 teeth and the sprocket has 20, with the pedals turning at 50 rpm. The sprocket is driven and has half the teeth, so it turns at 50 × 40 ÷ 20 = 100 rpm.

This is what the gear lever on a bicycle does. It moves the chain between sprockets of different sizes at the back. A large sprocket turns the back wheel slowly with a high torque, which suits a hill. A small one turns it fast with less torque, which suits the flat.

Sometimes a machine needs a big change of speed. A motor turning at 1,500 rpm may have to drive a drum at 100 rpm, a ratio of 15. One pair could do it, with a 10-tooth driver and a 150-tooth gear, but that big gear would be fifteen times as wide as the small one and the housing would have to be wider still.

A compound train gets the same ratio from two small pairs. The first pair's driven gear and the second pair's driver sit on the same shaft, so they are locked together and turn at the same speed. The first pair slows the speed by its ratio, and the second pair slows the result again.

afterFigure.text: In the figure the first pair has a ratio of 36 ÷ 12 = 3, which takes 1,500 rpm down to 500 rpm. The second has a ratio of 50 ÷ 10 = 5, which takes 500 rpm down to 100 rpm. The two ratios multiply: 3 × 5 = 15, and 1,500 ÷ 15 = 100 rpm. The torque rises by the same overall factor, from 4 N·m to 60 N·m. The largest gear in this box has 50 teeth, where one pair for the same ratio would need 150.

lead.text: Treat each pair as its own step. Find what it does to the speed, then hand that speed to the next pair.

lessons.orientation: Follow the turning from the pedals of a bicycle to its back wheel, and use tooth counts to find speed, torque and direction.
