blocks.text: Halfway up a steep hill you drop the bike into its lowest gear. The pedals go light, and your legs spin fast while the bike creeps forward. At the top you shift the other way. Now each push on a pedal is hard work, but one turn of the pedals carries you a long way down the road.

Nothing about you changed in between. All you changed was which pair of toothed wheels connects your feet to the back wheel. Last lesson a lever let a small force move a heavy load by moving through a longer distance. Gears do the same job for something that turns, and the trade is between how fast it spins and how hard it pushes.

This lesson follows the turning from the pedals to the back wheel. It starts with what two gears fix between them, then asks what happens to the push. After that it adds a third gear in the middle, a bicycle chain and two pairs of gears working together.

intro.promise: By the end you'll work out how fast and how hard the last wheel in a train of gears turns.

recap.keyIdea: Meshing gears pass teeth at the same rate, so speed × teeth is equal on both. An ideal mesh keeps the power, so torque rises by the ratio that speed falls.

blocks.text: You followed the turning from the pedals to the back wheel. A 20-tooth driver at 1,200 rpm turns a 60-tooth gear at 400 rpm, and the torque on that gear is three times the driver's. A chain obeys the same rule as a mesh and keeps the direction, while an idler turns the output the right way round and leaves the ratio alone.

In a compound train the ratios multiply, so two 3 : 1 pairs turn 1,800 rpm into 200 rpm in a box far smaller than one 9 : 1 pair would need. The bike is a train of gears with a chain in it, and shifting gear changes the ratio.

recap.nextHook: A real gearbox runs warm, because the teeth rub as they slide past each other and some of the energy turns into heat. The next lesson works out how much of the motor's effort reaches the last gear, and what that means for the size of motor you need.

lessons.title: Efficiency and power in a drive

lead.text: The first job is to measure how quickly a machine delivers energy. Take a winch that raises a 500 N crate by 3 m. The work done is the force times the distance, 500 × 3 = 1,500 J, and that is the same whether the winch takes five seconds or fifty. The difference between those two jobs is how hard the winch has to work.

The quantity that tells them apart is power, the work done each second. If the winch takes 5 s, its power is 1,500 ÷ 5 = 300 J per second. One joule per second is one watt, written W, so that is 300 W. The same number comes more directly from the speed. The crate rises 3 m in 5 s, which is 0.6 m/s, and force × speed = 500 × 0.6 = 300 W.

afterFigure.text: So in a straight line, power is force times speed. A winch that lifts the same crate twice as fast delivers twice the power, because it does the same work in half the time.

lead.text: Use force times speed. The winch in the question lifts at a steady rate, so one second of its work is enough.

A motor does not lift anything in a straight line. Its shaft turns, so its speed is given in revolutions per minute and its push is a torque. To get a power from those two, the speed of turning has to be written in a unit that fits with torque.

That unit uses the radian. Take a wheel of radius r and lay a piece of string of length r along its rim. The angle that string covers at the centre is one radian, a little under 60°. A full turn is the whole circumference, 2π × r, so it is 2π radians, about 6.28. The rate of turning in radians per second is the angular speed, written ω, the Greek letter omega.
To change rpm into rad/s, multiply by 2π, because each revolution is 2π radians, and divide by 60, because a minute has 60 seconds. A shaft at 120 rpm has ω = 120 × 2π ÷ 60 = 12.57 rad/s.
Each revolution is 2π radians, and a minute is 60 seconds. Put those two facts together.

steps.headline: The power of a turning shaft

lead.text: The winch idea carries over to a shaft. Picture a force F pushing round the rim of a wheel of radius r. The torque is F × r. When the shaft turns at ω radians per second, a point on the rim travels a distance r × ω each second, because a radian is the angle whose arc is as long as the radius.
Power is force times speed, so the power is F × rω. Regroup that as (F × r) × ω and it is the torque times the angular speed: P = T × ω.

afterFigure.text: Take a torque of 5 N·m at 120 rpm. The angular speed of 12.57 rad/s gives 5 × 12.57 ≈ 63 W. The radian is why the formula needs no extra factors, so the speed must be converted first. Putting 120 in directly would give 600, nearly ten times too large.

lead.text: The question gives the speed in rpm. The figure shows two motors with the same torque and different speeds.

steps.headline: A motor delivers 8 N·m at 3,000 rpm. Find its power output.

lead.text: Here is the same method for another motor.

workedSteps.text: Convert rpm to radians per second.
Multiply torque by angular speed.

lead.text: So far every shaft has passed on all of its power. A real mesh does not. The teeth rub as they roll over each other, and some of the work turns into heat and wear. Engineers describe this with efficiency, the fraction of the power put in that comes out as useful power. A mesh with an efficiency of 0.95, or 95%, passes on 95 W of every 100 W it receives.

A gearbox usually has several meshes in a row, and each pair of gears is called a stage. Each stage takes its share of what the one before delivered. Two stages at 90% leave 90% of 90%, which is 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81, or 81%. Taking 10% off twice would give 80%, which is wrong, because the second loss applies to what is left after the first.

afterFigure.text: The efficiencies multiply, so each added stage costs a few more per cent. That is the price of the extra torque. A third reduction stage lets the same motor turn the output with more torque, at a lower output speed and with a little less of the power arriving.

steps.headline: A gearbox has two meshes, each 95% efficient. Find the overall efficiency.

lead.text: Any number of stages multiply in the same way.

workedSteps.text: Each mesh passes on 0.95 of the power it receives.
Multiply the two efficiencies, then give the answer as a percentage.

lead.text: Losses change the output torque and leave the speed alone. The teeth still pass at the same rate, so a 4 : 1 gearbox still turns its output at exactly a quarter of the input speed, whatever the friction. The tooth counts fix the speed ratio.

Less power out at the same speed means less torque, since power is torque times speed. So the real output torque is the ideal output torque times the efficiency. Take 10 N·m going into a 3 : 1 pair that is 80% efficient. The ideal output is 10 × 3 = 30 N·m, and the real one is 30 × 0.8 = 24 N·m.
Find the ideal torque first, then take away what the losses cost.

The losses decide how big a motor to buy. The load receives only the useful power, and the motor supplies that plus whatever is lost on the way. So the motor has to supply the useful power divided by the machine's efficiency. A load that needs 600 W through a machine that is 75% efficient takes 600 ÷ 0.75 = 800 W from the motor, which is more than the load receives.

The same reasoning applies to force. A block and tackle with 4 strands has an ideal mechanical advantage of 4, but friction in the pulleys means some of the effort is wasted. The real mechanical advantage is the ideal one times the efficiency. At 75% that is 4 × 0.75 = 3, so a 900 N load needs an effort of 900 ÷ 3 = 300 N, where the ideal answer would have been 225 N.
Work out the power at the hook first. The motor must supply more than that.
