blocks.text: Put a hand on the casing of a gearbox that has been running for an hour and it is warm. The warmth is energy that went in at one end and never came out at the other. The teeth rub as they slide past each other, the bearings drag, and all that friction turns some of the motor's work into heat.

The last lesson let a pair of gears pass on everything it was given. That was a fair way to learn the rule, but a real machine always pays something, and the payment decides which motor you need to buy. Take a hoist that lifts a heavy load through a gearbox and a pulley. The motor has to supply the lift and the heat.

This lesson follows the energy from the load back to the motor. It first measures how quickly energy is delivered, in a straight line and then in a turning shaft. It then counts what each gear pair takes, and finishes by sizing the motor.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find what a turning shaft delivers, and the torque and motor size a real drive needs once friction takes its share.

recap.keyIdea: Power is torque times angular speed, with the speed in radians per second. Efficiencies multiply, and the motor supplies the useful power divided by the efficiency.

blocks.text: You started with a warm gearbox and followed the energy back from the hook. A shaft at 20 N·m and 1,500 rpm delivers 3,142 W once the speed is converted to 157.08 rad/s. Two meshes at 95% pass on 90.25% of the power, and a 90% efficient 4 : 1 gearbox gives 72 N·m.
For the hoist, lifting 2,000 N at 0.5 m/s is 1,000 W at the hook, so an 80% efficient system needs a motor that supplies 1,250 W. The heat in the casing is the difference.

recap.nextHook: You can now follow a force from a load back through pulleys and gears to a motor shaft, and say what each part keeps. Pick any machine and ask where the force goes and how much is lost on the way.

questions.prompt: A 10 kN force acts at 30° above the horizontal. Find its horizontal component, in kN, to two decimal places.
hints: The horizontal side of the triangle is next to the 30° angle.
Next to the angle means cosine: the share is F cos θ.
Calculate 10 × cos 30° and round to two decimal places.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Horizontal component = 10 cos 30° = 8.660 kN, which rounds to 8.66 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 8.66 kN. Next to the angle means cosine: the horizontal part is F cos θ.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 10 sin 30°, the vertical part. The horizontal side touches the angle, so use cosine.
That is the whole force. Only part of an angled force acts across.

questions.prompt: Vertical component (kN)
hints: Which side of the slope triangle is the rise?
The vertical share is rise over long side.
Multiply the pull by that share.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The slope triangle 3–4–5 gives sin θ = 3/5, so the vertical component is 5 × 3/5 = 3 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 3 kN: the pull times rise over long side. Any slope triangle gives the shares without a calculator.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the horizontal part: the run over the long side. The vertical part uses the rise.
That is the whole pull. Only a fraction of it acts upward.
The share is over the long side of the triangle, not over the run.

questions.prompt: A pin carries 3 kN acting horizontally and 4 kN acting vertically. Find the size of their resultant in kN.
hints: The forces are at right angles, so their sizes do not simply add.
Use Pythagoras on the two components.
Calculate √(3² + 4²).
questions.onCorrect: 5 kN. Square, add, root: the resultant is the long side of the force triangle.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes, which only works for forces on one line. These are at right angles.
That is the sum of the squares. Take the square root to get back to a force.

questions.prompt: A ring is held by 6 kN along +x and 8 kN along +y. What size, in kN, must a third force have to keep the ring in equilibrium?
hints: Equilibrium needs the sum of all forces to be zero.
The third force cancels the resultant of the other two.
Calculate √(6² + 8²).

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The third force must cancel the resultant of the first two: √(6² + 8²) = 10 kN, pointing opposite it.

questions.onCorrect: 10 kN, pointing opposite the resultant. A closed force polygon means equilibrium.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two sizes. They are at right angles, so find their resultant first.
That is the difference of the sizes. The forces are at right angles, not opposed.

questions.prompt: Forces of 12 kN along +x and 5 kN along +y act on the pin of a gusset plate. Find the size of their resultant in kN.
hints: Treat the two forces as perpendicular components.
Square each, add, then take the square root.
Calculate √(144 + 25).
questions.onCorrect: 13 kN. At right angles, square, add and take the root.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the sizes. At right angles they combine by Pythagoras.
That is the sum of the squares. The last step is the square root.

questions.prompt: A lamp hangs from two cables. Its free-body diagram isolates the lamp. Which force belongs on that diagram?

acceptedIdeas: The pull of each cable on the lamp
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The pull of each cable on the lamp. The cable pulls act on the lamp, so they belong on its diagram.

choices.label: The pull of each cable on the lamp
The pull of the lamp on the ceiling
The weight of the ceiling

questions.onCorrect: A free-body diagram holds only forces acting on the isolated body: here the lamp's weight and the two cable pulls.

misconceptions.feedback: That force acts on the ceiling, not on the lamp. Only forces on the isolated body belong.
The ceiling's weight acts on the ceiling. It does not act on the lamp.

questions.prompt: A 150 N force pushes at right angles to a spanner, 0.3 m from the bolt. Find the moment about the bolt in N·m.
hints: The push is already at right angles, so the full distance counts.
Multiply force by perpendicular distance.
Calculate 150 × 0.3.
questions.onCorrect: 45 N·m: force times perpendicular distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force alone. A moment multiplies it by the distance too.
That divides the force by the distance. A moment multiplies them.

questions.prompt: Moment (N·m)
hints: The turning part is 75 N. How far along the spanner does it act?
Multiply the turning part by the distance.
Calculate 75 × 0.3.
questions.onCorrect: 22.5 N·m: less than at right angles, because only part of the push turns the spanner.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the moment for a push at right angles. At 30° only part of it turns the spanner.
That uses cos 30°, the part along the handle, which does not turn it.

questions.prompt: A 200 N force pulls along a spanner's handle, directly away from the bolt, at a point 0.3 m from it. Find its moment about the bolt in N·m.
hints: Sketch the line of action of the force.
Measure the perpendicular distance from the bolt to that line.
Multiply the force by that distance.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The line of action passes through the bolt, so the perpendicular distance and the moment are both zero.

questions.onCorrect: A line of action through the pivot has no arm, so the moment vanishes whatever the force.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies the force by the distance along the handle. A moment uses the distance at right angles to the line of action.

questions.prompt: A 300 N child sits 2 m left of a see-saw's pivot. How far right of the pivot, in metres, must a 400 N child sit for the see-saw to balance?
hints: The two moments about the pivot must be equal and opposite.
Find the left child's moment, then divide by the right child's weight.
Calculate 300 × 2 ÷ 400.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Balance needs 400 × d = 300 × 2 = 600 N·m, so d = 1.5 m.

questions.onCorrect: 1.5 m. The heavier child sits closer, so that both moments are equal.

misconceptions.feedback: Equal distances only balance equal weights. The heavier child needs a shorter arm.
That divides by the wrong weight. Divide the left moment by the right child's weight.

questions.prompt: A door handle is 0.8 m from the hinges. It is pulled with 40 N at right angles to the door. Find the moment about the hinges in N·m.
hints: The hinge line is the pivot.
The pull is perpendicular, so use the full 0.8 m.
Calculate 40 × 0.8.
questions.onCorrect: 32 N·m: force times its perpendicular distance from the hinges.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the force and the distance. A moment multiplies them.
That divides the force by the distance. A moment multiplies them.

questions.prompt: To loosen a tight nut with the least effort, where and how should you push on the spanner?
hints: Moment is force times perpendicular distance. Make that distance as large as you can.

acceptedIdeas: At the end of the handle, at right angles to it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: At the end of the handle, at right angles to it. The largest perpendicular distance gives the largest moment, and only a push at right angles uses all of it.

choices.label: At the end of the handle, at right angles to it
Near the nut, at right angles to the handle
At the end of the handle, along its length

questions.onCorrect: The largest perpendicular distance gives the largest moment for a given force.

misconceptions.feedback: Near the nut the arm is short, so the same push gives a small moment.
A push along the handle passes through the nut and has no arm.

questions.prompt: A 6 m beam rests on a pin at A (x = 0) and a roller at B (x = 6 m). It carries 12 kN at x = 2 m. Take moments about A to find the reaction at B in kN.
hints: Taking moments about A removes the reaction at A from the equation.
The load's moment about A must equal B's moment about A.
Calculate 12 × 2 ÷ 6.
questions.onCorrect: 4 kN. Moments about A balance the load against RB, and the reaction at A drops out.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the load's moment about A, in kN·m. Divide by the distance between the supports to get a force.
That is the reaction at A, the nearer support. Moments about A give the other one.

questions.prompt: Reaction at A (kN)
hints: The two reactions together carry the whole load.
What is the load, and how much does B take?
Calculate 12 − 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: RA = 12 − RB = 12 − 4 = 8 kN. Moments about B confirm it: 12 × 4 ÷ 6 = 8 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 8 kN. A is nearer the load, so it carries more: the reactions add up to the load.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reaction at B. A is nearer the load, so it carries more.
That would be the share if the load sat at the middle. This load is nearer A.

questions.prompt: A 6 m beam on supports at x = 0 and x = 6 m carries 4 kN/m over its first 3 m. Find the reaction at the right-hand support in kN.
hints: Replace the spread load by its total acting at the middle of the loaded length.
Take moments about the left support.
Calculate (4 × 3) × 1.5 ÷ 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The spread load totals 4 × 3 = 12 kN acting at x = 1.5 m. About the left support: 6R = 12 × 1.5, so R = 3 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 3 kN. The spread load acts as one force at its middle, so the right support takes the smaller share.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the total of the spread load. Its moment about the left support needs its arm at the middle of the loaded length.
That is the left reaction. The question asks for the right-hand support.
That shares the total equally, but the load sits only on the left half.

questions.prompt: A beam has supports at x = 0 and x = 4 m and a 10 kN load at its free end, x = 6 m. Taking upward as positive, find the reaction at x = 0 in kN.
hints: Find the reaction at x = 4 m first, by moments about x = 0.
Then the two reactions must add to the 10 kN load.
Calculate 10 − 10 × 6 ÷ 4, keeping the sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About x = 0: 4RB = 10 × 6, so RB = 15 kN. Then RA = 10 − 15 = −5 kN: the left support pulls down.

questions.onCorrect: A negative reaction means the support holds the beam down. The overhanging load levers the far end up.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign. With upward positive, a support that holds the beam down is negative.
That is the reaction at the other support. Subtract it from the load to get this one.

questions.prompt: A 10 m beam on supports at its ends carries 20 kN at x = 3 m and 10 kN at x = 8 m. Find the left reaction in kN.
hints: Take moments about the right-hand support to remove its reaction.
Measure each load's distance from x = 10 m.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: About the right support: 10RA = 20 × 7 + 10 × 2 = 160, so RA = 16 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 16 kN. Moments about the far support: each load's force times its distance from it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the other reaction. The question asks for the left one.
That is the sum of the moments. Divide by the span to get a force.

questions.prompt: Name the support that stops a beam moving vertically but lets it slide horizontally and rotate.
hints: One support of a simply supported beam is free to slide so the beam can expand.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A roller support: it pushes at right angles to its surface and nothing more.

questions.onCorrect: A roller pushes at right angles to its surface and nothing more.

misconceptions.feedback: A pin also stops sliding. The support described lets the beam slide.
A fixed support stops rotation too. This one lets the beam rotate.

questions.prompt: A triangular truss spans 4 m with its apex C 1.5 m above the supports, so each sloping member is 2.5 m long. A 12 kN load hangs from C. Find the size of the force in member AC in kN.
hints: Isolate joint C. Two equal member forces meet there.
Each contributes a vertical part of F × rise/length.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At C, both sloping members have vertical parts of F × 1.5/2.5. Then 2 × 0.6F = 12, so F = 10 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 10 kN. Each member's vertical part is only 0.6 of its force, so the slanting members carry more than half the load each.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the second sloping member. Both share the load.
That is each member's vertical share. The member itself carries more, because it slants.

questions.prompt: A triangular truss carries a load at its apex, and its two sloping members push outward on the feet. Is the bottom member AB, which joins the feet, in tension or compression?
hints: Picture the sloping members spreading under the load. What must AB do to stop the feet moving apart?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Tension: AB pulls inward to stop the supports spreading apart.

questions.onCorrect: AB pulls the feet together: a member that pulls on its joints is in tension.

misconceptions.feedback: A member in compression pushes on its joints. AB has to stop the feet spreading, so think about which way it acts on them.

questions.prompt: Force in AB (kN)
hints: AB cancels the horizontal part of AC's push.
That part is the force times run over length.
Calculate 10 × 2/2.5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Horizontal balance at A: FAB = 10 × 2/2.5 = 8 kN, in tension.

questions.onCorrect: 8 kN. The bottom member balances only the horizontal part of the push of AC.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force in AC, along the slope. AB balances only its horizontal part.
That is the vertical part. AB has to cancel the horizontal part.

questions.prompt: A king-post truss adds a vertical member DC from the middle of the bottom chord, D, up to the apex C. The only load is 12 kN at C. Find the force in DC in kN.
hints: Isolate joint D and list the members meeting there.
AD and DB lie on one straight line; DC is the only member with a vertical part.
Write ΣFy = 0 at D with no load applied there.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At D, AD and DB are collinear and horizontal and no load acts, so vertical balance leaves DC with no force.

questions.onCorrect: DC carries nothing: at an unloaded joint, only DC has a vertical part, so it must be zero.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the applied load, but it acts at C, not at D.

questions.prompt: A triangular truss spans 3 m with its apex 2 m high, so each sloping member is 2.5 m long. A 16 kN load acts at the apex. Find the tension in the bottom member in kN.
hints: Find the sloping member force first, at the apex.
Then use horizontal balance at a support joint.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the apex: 2F × 2/2.5 = 16, so F = 10 kN in each sloping member. At a support: tension = 10 × 1.5/2.5 = 6 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 6 kN. The apex gives the sloping force; the horizontal part of it is what the bottom member balances.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force in each sloping member. The bottom member balances only the horizontal part.
That is the vertical part of a sloping member. The bottom member balances the horizontal part.

questions.prompt: A member pushes outward on the joints at both its ends. What is it in: tension or compression?
hints: Ask whether the member is being stretched or squashed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Compression: a strut pushes on its joints.

questions.onCorrect: A member that pushes on its joints is squashed: compression.

misconceptions.feedback: A member in tension pulls on its joints. This one pushes them.

questions.prompt: A steel bar with a cross-section of 400 mm² carries a 20 kN axial pull. Find the stress in MPa.
hints: Convert the load to newtons.
Divide by the area in mm²; 1 N/mm² is 1 MPa.
Calculate 20,000 ÷ 400.
questions.onCorrect: 50 MPa: force in newtons over area in square millimetres gives megapascals directly.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves the load in kN, so it is a thousand times too small. Convert to newtons first.
That is the force in newtons. Divide it by the area.

questions.prompt: Stretch (mm)
hints: Stretch is strain times original length.
Use the length in mm.
questions.onCorrect: 0.5 mm: strain times original length. Steel barely stretches, and a strain gauge can still measure it.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the strain, a ratio. Multiply by the length to get a stretch.
Check E: 200 GPa is 200,000 MPa, a thousand times more than 200.

questions.prompt: An aluminium bar (E = 70 GPa) 1,400 mm long carries a stress of 50 MPa. Find its stretch in mm.
hints: Write E in MPa: 70 GPa is 70,000 MPa.
Strain = stress ÷ E, then multiply by length.
questions.onCorrect: 1 mm. The aluminium bar is shorter than the steel one yet stretches twice as far, because E is lower.

misconceptions.feedback: E must be in MPa to match the stress: 70 GPa is 70,000 MPa.
That is the steel bar's stretch over 2,000 mm. Aluminium is less stiff and this bar is shorter.

questions.prompt: A steel bar with yield stress 250 MPa and ultimate strength 400 MPa is loaded to 300 MPa, then unloaded. What happens?
hints: Compare 300 MPa with both strengths.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It keeps a permanent stretch. 300 MPa is past yield but below the ultimate strength, so the bar survives with a permanent set.

choices.label: It returns to its original length
It keeps a permanent stretch
It has already fractured

questions.onCorrect: 300 MPa is past yield but below the ultimate strength, so the bar survives with a permanent set.

misconceptions.feedback: A bar only springs back fully below its yield stress. This load is above it.
Fracture needs the ultimate strength. This load is below it.

questions.prompt: A square rod 10 mm × 10 mm carries a 15 kN axial pull. Find the stress in MPa.
hints: Find the cross-sectional area first.
Convert the load to newtons and divide.
questions.onCorrect: 150 MPa: area first, then force in newtons over that area.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force in newtons. Divide it by the area.
That divides by the side, 10 mm, not by the area. Multiply the two sides first.

questions.prompt: A steel tie (E = 200 GPa) 5 m long works at 100 MPa. Find its stretch in mm.
hints: Convert the length to millimetres.
Strain = stress ÷ E with E in MPa.
questions.onCorrect: 2.5 mm: strain 0.0005 over 5,000 mm. Convert the length so that the units agree.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves the length in metres. The answer is wanted in mm.
Check E: use 200,000 MPa, not 200.

questions.prompt: A steel tie with yield stress 250 MPa and area 400 mm² carries 40 kN. Find its factor of safety against yield.
hints: Find the working stress first.
Divide the yield stress by the working stress.
questions.onCorrect: 2.5: the tie could take two and a half times its working stress before yielding.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the working stress. Compare it with the yield stress.
That is working stress over yield stress, upside down. The factor is more than one.

questions.prompt: Minimum area (mm²)
hints: Area is load divided by allowable stress.
Use the load in newtons.
Calculate 60,000 ÷ 125.
questions.onCorrect: 480 mm²: the load in newtons over the allowable stress.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the factor instead of dividing. The allowable stress is lower than yield.
That ignores the factor of safety. Divide the yield stress by it first.

questions.prompt: Square steel bars come with 20, 25 and 30 mm sides. Which side length, in mm, is the smallest that gives at least 480 mm² of area?
hints: Work out the area of each bar.
Discard any below the required area.
Pick the smallest remaining side.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Areas are 20 × 20 = 400, 25 × 25 = 625 and 30 × 30 = 900 mm². 400 mm² is too small, so the 25 mm bar is the lightest that works.

questions.onCorrect: 25 mm: the smallest stock bar that meets the area. Rounding up costs a little weight and gains margin.

misconceptions.feedback: That bar's area is below the area needed, so it would be overstressed.
That works, but it is heavier than needed. Choose the smallest bar that does.

questions.prompt: A 25 mm square steel tie (625 mm²) is 3 m long and carries 60 kN. With E = 200 GPa, find its stretch in mm.
hints: Find the stress in MPa.
Strain = stress ÷ 200,000 MPa; multiply by 3,000 mm.
questions.onCorrect: 1.44 mm. Safe against yield does not mean stiff enough: check the stretch against what the connection allows.

misconceptions.feedback: Check E: use 200,000 MPa, not 200.
That is the stress in MPa. Divide by E and multiply by the length to get a stretch.

questions.prompt: A steel with yield stress 355 MPa is used with a factor of safety of 2.5. Find the allowable working stress in MPa.
hints: The factor of safety divides the failure stress.
Allowable = yield ÷ FoS.
Calculate 355 ÷ 2.5.
questions.onCorrect: 142 MPa: the yield stress divided by the factor of safety.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the factor. The allowable stress is below yield, so divide.

questions.prompt: A 300 mm² bar of steel that yields at 250 MPa must keep a factor of safety of 1.5. Find the largest axial load it may carry, in kN.
hints: Find the allowable stress.
Load = allowable stress × area, in newtons.
Calculate 300 × 250 ÷ 1.5, then convert to kN.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Allowable stress = 250 ÷ 1.5 MPa; load = 300 × 250 ÷ 1.5 = 50,000 N = 50 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 50 kN: allowable stress times area, converted from newtons.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores the factor of safety. The allowable stress is yield divided by it.
That is the load in newtons. The answer is wanted in kN.

questions.prompt: A 6 m beam on end supports carries 12 kN at x = 2 m, so the reactions are 8 kN at A and 4 kN at B. Find the shear force just to the right of the load, in kN, counting upward forces on the left piece as positive.
hints: Add the vertical forces on the piece to the left of the cut.
Just right of the load, both the reaction at A and the load are on the left piece.
Calculate 8 − 12, keeping the sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Left of the cut: +8 kN reaction and −12 kN load, so V = 8 − 12 = −4 kN.

questions.onCorrect: −4 kN. The downward load outweighs the reaction, so the shear changes sign across it.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign: the load is downward, so just to its right the shear is negative.
That is the shear just left of the load. Just to its right the load is on the left piece too.

questions.prompt: Bending moment (kN·m)
hints: Only the left reaction is on the left piece.
Multiply that force by its distance from the cut.
Calculate 8 × 2.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only RA acts left of the cut: M = 8 × 2 = 16 kN·m, sagging.

questions.onCorrect: 16 kN·m: the left reaction times its distance. The crate itself acts at the cut, so it adds no moment.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the reaction, not a moment. Multiply it by its distance from the cut.
That uses the crate's weight, but the crate acts at the cut and adds no moment.

questions.prompt: An 8 m beam on end supports carries a uniform 3 kN/m along its full length. Find the largest bending moment, in kN·m.
hints: By symmetry the peak is at midspan.
Use wL²/8, or balance the left half about the cut.
Calculate 3 × 8² ÷ 8.
questions.onCorrect: 24 kN·m at midspan: wL²/8, or the left half balanced about the cut.

misconceptions.feedback: That is wL² without dividing by eight.
That is each reaction, a force. The peak moment multiplies forces by distances.

questions.prompt: Along a simply supported beam, what is the shear force where the bending moment reaches its peak? Answer in one word.
hints: The slope of the moment diagram equals the shear force.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Zero: the moment's slope is the shear, and the slope vanishes at the peak.

questions.onCorrect: At the top of the moment curve the slope is level, so the shear there is nothing.

misconceptions.feedback: At the top of a hump the curve is neither rising nor falling. Shear is its slope, so ask which value means a level slope.

questions.prompt: A 3 m cantilever carries 5 kN at its free end. Find the size of the bending moment at the wall, in kN·m.
hints: Cut at the wall and look at the free piece.
Only the end load acts on it.
Calculate 5 × 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The load acts 3 m from the wall: M = 5 × 3 = 15 kN·m, hogging.

questions.onCorrect: 15 kN·m: the free piece has one force, so the moment is that force times its distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the force. Multiply it by its distance from the wall.
That adds force and distance. A moment multiplies them.

questions.prompt: A 10 m beam on end supports carries 20 kN at midspan. Find the largest bending moment, in kN·m.
hints: Find the reactions by symmetry.
The peak is under the load.
Calculate 10 × 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each reaction is 10 kN; under the load M = 10 × 5 = 50 kN·m. This is PL/4.

questions.onCorrect: 50 kN·m under the load: one reaction times its 5 m distance, which is PL/4.

misconceptions.feedback: That is each reaction. Multiply by its distance from the load to get a moment.
That multiplies the reaction by the whole span. The distance to the cut is half of it.

questions.prompt: A solid rectangular beam 100 mm wide and 200 mm deep carries a bending moment of 20 kN·m. Its second moment of area is bh³/12. Find the largest bending stress, in MPa.
hints: Convert the moment to N·mm: 1 kN·m = 10⁶ N·mm.
The outer fibre is half the depth from the neutral axis.
questions.onCorrect: 30 MPa: σ = My/I, with the moment in N·mm and y half the depth.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the full depth, 200 mm, for y. The outer fibre is half the depth from the neutral axis.

questions.prompt: Largest stress (MPa)
hints: Use M = 20 × 10⁶ N·mm and y = 50 mm.
Divide M × y by I.
questions.onCorrect: 60 MPa, double the on-edge value: I falls to a quarter while y only halves.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the stress with the beam on edge. Laid flat, I is smaller and the outer fibre is closer.
That keeps y at the old 100 mm. Laid flat, the depth is 100 mm, so y is half of that.

questions.prompt: Find the second moment of area of a rectangle 60 mm wide and 100 mm deep about its horizontal centroidal axis, in units of 10⁶ mm⁴.
hints: Use I = bh³/12 with h the depth.
Cube the depth before multiplying by the width.
Calculate 60 × 1,000,000 ÷ 12, then divide by 10⁶.
questions.onCorrect: 5 × 10⁶ mm⁴: width times depth cubed, over twelve.

misconceptions.feedback: That is I in mm⁴. The question asks in units of 10⁶ mm⁴, so divide by 10⁶.

questions.prompt: An I-section is 200 mm deep with 100 mm wide, 10 mm thick flanges and a 6 mm web. Its I is the outer rectangle minus the two empty side regions: (100 × 200³ − 94 × 180³)/12. Find I in units of 10⁶ mm⁴, to two decimal places.
hints: Each empty region is 47 mm wide; together they are 94 mm wide and 180 mm deep.
Subtract their combined bh³ from the outer rectangle's.
Divide the difference by 12 and by 10⁶.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 × 200³ = 800 × 10⁶ and 94 × 180³ = 548.2 × 10⁶; the difference over 12 is 20.98 × 10⁶ mm⁴.

questions.onCorrect: 20.98 × 10⁶ mm⁴: about a third of the solid rectangle's I, from about a sixth of the material.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the solid rectangle. Subtract the empty side regions first.
That is the difference before dividing by twelve.

questions.prompt: A square beam 100 mm × 100 mm carries 5 kN·m. Find the largest bending stress in MPa.
hints: Find I for the square with bh³/12.
The outer fibre is 50 mm from the axis.
questions.onCorrect: 30 MPa: I for the square, then σ = My/I with y half the depth.

misconceptions.feedback: That uses the full depth for y. The outer fibre is half the depth from the neutral axis.

questions.prompt: Name the line through a bent beam's cross-section where the bending stress is zero.
hints: Fibres on one side are stretched and on the other squashed. What lies between?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The neutral axis, which passes through the centroid of the section.

questions.onCorrect: The neutral axis passes through the centroid and carries no bending stress.

misconceptions.feedback: That line does sit in the middle, but it has a specific name. What do engineers call the line of zero bending stress?

questions.prompt: A steel cantilever 2 m long (E = 200 GPa, I = 2 × 10⁶ mm⁴) carries 3 kN at its tip. Using δ = PL³/3EI, find the tip deflection in mm.
hints: Convert to N, m, Pa and m⁴: 10⁶ mm⁴ is 10⁻⁶ m⁴.
Compute EI first, then PL³/3EI in metres.
Calculate 3,000 × 2³ ÷ (3 × 400,000), then convert to mm.
questions.onCorrect: 20 mm: base units throughout, then metres converted to millimetres.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the deflection in metres. Convert it to mm.
That leaves out the 3 in the denominator, 3EI.

questions.prompt: Keep the load and section but double the cantilever's length. By what factor does the tip deflection grow?
hints: Only L changes in PL³/3EI.
Deflection depends on the cube of length.
Multiply 2 by itself three times.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: δ ∝ L³, so doubling L multiplies δ by 2³ = 8.

questions.onCorrect: Eightfold: deflection depends on the cube of length, so long spans are governed by stiffness.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by 3. Cubing means 2 × 2 × 2.
That is the factor for doubling the load. Length is cubed.
That squares the length. In PL³/3EI it is cubed.

questions.prompt: Tip deflection (mm)
hints: Divide PL³ by 3EI.
The result is in metres.
Calculate 2,100 ÷ 210,000, then convert to mm.
questions.onCorrect: 10 mm. Aluminium's lower E makes a section bend about 2.9 times as much as steel.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the deflection in metres. Convert it to mm.

questions.prompt: For the 2 m steel cantilever (E = 200 GPa, I = 2 × 10⁶ mm⁴), find the tip stiffness k = 3EI/L³ in kN/m.
hints: EI is 400,000 N·m².
Divide 3EI by L³.
Calculate 3 × 400,000 ÷ 8, then convert N/m to kN/m.
questions.onCorrect: 150 kN/m, which agrees with the 3 kN producing 20 mm. Stiffness falls with the cube of the length.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in N/m. The question wants kN/m.
That leaves out the 3 in 3EI/L³.

questions.prompt: A 2 m steel cantilever (E = 200 GPa) carries 3 kN at its tip, and its deflection is limited to 8 mm. Find the minimum I, in units of 10⁶ mm⁴.
hints: Rearrange δ = PL³/3EI for I.
Keep δ in metres and E in pascals.
Calculate 24,000 ÷ (4.8 × 10⁹), then convert m⁴ to 10⁶ mm⁴.
questions.onCorrect: 5 × 10⁶ mm⁴: rearrange for I, keep base units, then convert.

misconceptions.feedback: That is I in mm⁴. The question asks in units of 10⁶ mm⁴.

questions.prompt: Which single change halves a cantilever's tip deflection under the same load?
hints: Look at where each quantity sits in PL³/3EI.

acceptedIdeas: Doubling the second moment of area
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Doubling the second moment of area. δ = PL³/3EI, so doubling I halves δ.

choices.label: Doubling the second moment of area
Doubling the length
Halving Young's modulus

questions.onCorrect: I is in the denominator, so doubling it halves δ. Doubling L multiplies δ by eight; halving E doubles it.

misconceptions.feedback: Length is cubed in PL³/3EI, and it sits on top, so doubling it makes things much worse.
E is in the denominator, so halving it doubles the deflection.

questions.prompt: A crowbar is levered over a fulcrum. The hand pushes 1.2 m from the fulcrum and the load sits 0.2 m from it. Find the mechanical advantage.
hints: Mechanical advantage is load force over effort force.
For a balanced lever, that equals the ratio of the arms.
Calculate 1.2 ÷ 0.2.
questions.onCorrect: 6: the effort arm is six times the load arm, so the load force is six times the effort.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the arms. Mechanical advantage is a ratio.
That is the ratio upside down. Here the effort arm is the longer one.

questions.prompt: Effort (N)
hints: Divide the load's moment by the effort arm.
The load's moment is 180 N·m.
Calculate 180 ÷ 1.2.
questions.onCorrect: 150 N holds a 900 N load: the long arm trades distance for force.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the mechanical advantage. A lever reduces the effort needed.
That is the load. The effort is smaller, because the long arm helps.

questions.prompt: A pulley system has 4 rope strands supporting the moving block, which carries an 800 N load. Ignoring friction and the block's weight, find the effort in newtons.
hints: The rope tension is the same in every strand.
The supporting strands share the load equally.
Calculate 800 ÷ 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 4 strands carries the rope tension: effort = 800 ÷ 4 = 200 N.

questions.onCorrect: 200 N: the supporting strands share the load, so the effort is the load divided by their number.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the number of strands. They share the load, so divide.
That is the load, not the effort. The strands share it.

questions.prompt: To lift an 800 N load 0.5 m with 4 supporting strands, how many metres of rope must be pulled?
hints: Every supporting strand gets shorter by the lift height.
The rope taken up comes out through the hand.
Calculate 4 × 0.5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each strand shortens by 0.5 m: 4 × 0.5 = 2 m.

questions.onCorrect: 2 m: four strands each shorten by the lift. Less force costs more rope.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides. Every strand shortens by the lift, so multiply by the number of strands.
That is the lift. The rope pulled through is more than that.

questions.prompt: In the forearm, the biceps attaches 0.04 m from the elbow, and a 50 N weight is held in the hand 0.32 m from the elbow. Treating the forearm as a weightless horizontal lever, find the biceps force in newtons.
hints: The elbow is the fulcrum.
Balance moments: effort × effort arm = load × load arm.
Calculate 50 × 0.32 ÷ 0.04.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Biceps × 0.04 = 50 × 0.32, so the biceps pulls 16 ÷ 0.04 = 400 N, eight times the weight held.

questions.onCorrect: 400 N: here the effort arm is the short one, so the effort is larger than the load.

misconceptions.feedback: That inverts the ratio. The effort arm is the shorter arm, so the effort must be the larger force.
That is the weight's moment about the elbow in N·m. Divide by the biceps arm to get a force.

questions.prompt: A wheelbarrow has its load between the wheel axle and the handles. Which class of lever is it: first, second or third?
hints: Locate the fulcrum first, then see which of load and effort lies between.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Second class: the load sits between the fulcrum and the effort.

questions.onCorrect: The load sits between the fulcrum and the effort: second class.

misconceptions.feedback: A first-class lever has the fulcrum in the middle, like a seesaw.
A third-class lever has the effort in the middle. In a wheelbarrow the effort is at the handles, at the end.

questions.prompt: A 20-tooth driver gear turning at 1,200 rpm meshes with a 60-tooth gear. Find the output speed in rpm.
hints: Speed × teeth is equal on both gears.
The bigger gear turns more slowly.
Calculate 1,200 × 20 ÷ 60.
questions.onCorrect: 400 rpm: speed × teeth is equal, so three times the teeth means a third of the speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the ratio, which speeds the larger gear up. The larger gear turns more slowly.
That is the driver's speed. The gears have different teeth, so their speeds differ.

questions.prompt: Find the output torque in N·m.
hints: Torque rises by the gear ratio.
What is the ratio of driven teeth to driver teeth?
Multiply the input torque by that ratio.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Torque rises by the ratio 60/20 = 3: 10 × 3 = 30 N·m.

questions.onCorrect: 30 N·m: a third of the speed means three times the torque.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the ratio. Torque rises as speed falls.
That is the input torque. A slower output shaft carries more.

questions.prompt: A 30-tooth idler is placed between the 20-tooth driver, turning at 1,200 rpm, and the 60-tooth output. Find the idler's speed in rpm.
hints: The idler is driven directly by the 20-tooth gear.
Speed × teeth is equal across that mesh.
Calculate 1,200 × 20 ÷ 30.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The idler meshes with the driver: 1,200 × 20 ÷ 30 = 800 rpm. The output still turns at 1,200 × 20 ÷ 60 = 400 rpm.

questions.onCorrect: 800 rpm: the idler follows the usual rule across its own mesh with the driver.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the output gear's speed. The idler is driven by the 20-tooth gear.

questions.prompt: A compound train has 15 teeth driving 45, then, on the same shaft, 20 teeth driving 60. The input turns at 1,800 rpm. Find the output speed in rpm.
hints: Find each stage's ratio, driven over driver.
Multiply the stage ratios for a compound train.
Calculate 1,800 ÷ (3 × 3).
questions.onCorrect: 200 rpm: stage ratios multiply, so two 3 : 1 stages give 9 : 1 in a small box.

misconceptions.feedback: That applies only one stage. A compound train has two, and the ratios multiply.

questions.prompt: A bicycle's 48-tooth chainring drives a 16-tooth rear sprocket. The pedals turn at 60 rpm. Find the rear wheel's speed in rpm.
hints: The chain carries teeth past both sprockets at the same rate.
Speed × teeth is equal on both.
Calculate 60 × 48 ÷ 16.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: A chain works like a mesh: 60 × 48 ÷ 16 = 180 rpm. Here the smaller sprocket is driven, so it turns faster.

questions.onCorrect: 180 rpm: the driven sprocket has fewer teeth, so it turns faster.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the ratio. The driven sprocket is the smaller one, so it turns faster.

questions.prompt: A 20-tooth driver turns a 60-tooth output through a 30-tooth idler. Compared with the driver, which way does the output turn: same or opposite?
hints: Each pair of meshing external gears turns in opposite senses. Count the meshes.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same way: each external mesh reverses rotation, and there are two meshes.

questions.onCorrect: Two meshes, so two reversals: the output turns the same way as the driver.

misconceptions.feedback: Count the meshes. The idler meshes with both the driver and the output, and each mesh reverses the rotation.

questions.prompt: A motor delivers 20 N·m at 1,500 rpm. Find its power output in watts, to the nearest watt.
hints: Convert rpm to radians per second: multiply by 2π and divide by 60.
Power is torque times angular speed.
Calculate 20 × 1,500 × 2π ÷ 60 and round.
questions.onCorrect: About 3,142 W: torque times angular speed, with the speed in radians per second.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies torque by speed in rpm. Convert rpm to radians per second first.

questions.prompt: Find the overall efficiency as a percentage.
hints: Write each stage as a decimal.
Multiply the two efficiencies.
Calculate 0.95 × 0.95, then convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 90.25%: multiplying keeps track of the power left after each stage.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts 5% twice. Each stage passes on 95% of what it receives, so multiply.
That is one stage. There are two, and their efficiencies multiply.

questions.prompt: A single-stage gearbox with a 4 : 1 reduction is 90% efficient. The input torque is 20 N·m. Find the output torque in N·m.
hints: Start from the ideal torque multiplication.
Losses reduce torque because the speed ratio is fixed by the teeth.
Calculate 20 × 4 × 0.9.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Ideal output 20 × 4 = 80 N·m; with losses 80 × 0.9 = 72 N·m.

questions.onCorrect: 72 N·m: the ideal torque times the efficiency, since the speed ratio is fixed by the teeth.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ideal torque. Losses reduce it.
That applies the efficiency but not the 4 : 1 ratio.

questions.prompt: A hoist lifts 2,000 N at 0.5 m/s through a pulley system that is 80% efficient overall. Find the power the motor must supply, in watts.
hints: Useful power is force times speed.
Input power is useful power divided by efficiency.
questions.onCorrect: 1,250 W: the motor supplies the useful power divided by the efficiency.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the useful power at the hook. Losses mean the motor supplies more.
That multiplies by the efficiency. The motor supplies more than the hook receives, so divide.

questions.prompt: A block and tackle with 4 supporting strands is 80% efficient. Find the effort needed to raise a 1,600 N load, in N.
hints: The ideal effort is load divided by the number of strands.
Friction means the real effort is larger: divide by the efficiency too.
questions.onCorrect: 500 N: the real mechanical advantage is the ideal 4 times the efficiency.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the ideal effort. Friction makes the real effort bigger.
That multiplies by the efficiency. Friction raises the effort, so divide.

questions.prompt: A designer adds a third reduction stage so that the same motor delivers more output torque. What is given up?
hints: Output power can never exceed input power.

acceptedIdeas: Output speed, plus a little extra loss
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Output speed, plus a little extra loss. More reduction multiplies torque by slowing the output, and each extra mesh wastes more power.

choices.label: Output speed, plus a little extra loss
Input power
Nothing: the torque comes free

questions.onCorrect: More reduction multiplies torque by slowing the output, and each extra mesh wastes a few more per cent of the power.

misconceptions.feedback: The motor sets the input power. A third stage changes what the output does with it.
Torque is never free. More torque costs speed, and each stage adds loss.

questions.prompt: A 100 mm × 200 mm timber plank is to be used as a floor joist. Which way up makes the stiffer joist?
hints: Think of bending a ruler flat, then on edge.

acceptedIdeas: Standing on its 100 mm edge, 200 mm deep
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Standing on its 100 mm edge, 200 mm deep. On edge the plank is 200 mm deep, and depth matters far more than width in bending.

choices.label: Standing on its 100 mm edge, 200 mm deep
Lying flat, 100 mm deep
There is no difference

questions.onCorrect: Standing on edge is stiffer: the depth is cubed in I, and on edge the plank is 200 mm deep.

misconceptions.feedback: Lying flat puts the material close to the middle, where it does little. Try bending a ruler both ways.
Try bending a ruler flat and on edge. The difference is large.

questions.prompt: A symmetric section is 120 mm deep. How far, in mm, is its outer fibre from the neutral axis?
hints: Where does the neutral axis of a symmetric section sit?
It is at mid-depth.
Take half of the depth.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The neutral axis is at mid-depth, so the outer fibre is 120 ÷ 2 = 60 mm from it.

questions.onCorrect: 60 mm. In a symmetric section the neutral axis is at mid-depth, so y is half the depth.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole depth. The neutral axis is at the middle, so the outer fibre is half of it out.

questions.prompt: Why is the stress largest at the outer fibre?
hints: What does σ = My/I say about y?

acceptedIdeas: Stress grows with distance from the neutral axis, and the outer fibre is furthest.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stress grows with distance from the neutral axis, and the outer fibre is furthest.. σ grows with y, and the outer fibre has the largest y.

choices.label: Stress grows with distance from the neutral axis, and the outer fibre is furthest.
The outer fibre carries all of the load.
I is largest at the surface.

questions.onCorrect: σ = My/I rises with y, so the fibre furthest from the neutral axis works hardest.

misconceptions.feedback: Every fibre carries some load, but those near the neutral axis carry very little.
I is one number for the whole section. It does not change with position.

questions.prompt: A rectangular beam's depth is doubled and its width is unchanged. By what factor does its second moment of area change?
hints: In bh³/12, which letter changes?
What happens to h³ when h doubles?
Multiply 2 by itself three times.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: I = bh³/12, so doubling h multiplies I by 2³ = 8.

questions.onCorrect: I rises eightfold: depth is cubed, which is why deep sections are so much stiffer.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the factor for doubling the width. Depth is cubed in bh³/12.
That squares the depth. In bh³/12 the depth is cubed.

questions.prompt: A cantilever carries 3 kN at its tip and sags 20 mm. The steel stays elastic. How far, in mm, would it sag under 6 kN at its tip?
hints: Elastic means deflection is proportional to load.
The load has doubled.
Double the deflection.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: In the elastic range deflection is proportional to load, so doubling the load doubles the sag: 2 × 20 = 40 mm.

questions.onCorrect: 40 mm. In the elastic range, deflection is proportional to load.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the sag under 3 kN. Twice the load bends it further.
That halves the sag. More load bends the cantilever more.

questions.prompt: A section has E = 200 GPa and I = 2 × 10⁻⁶ m⁴. Find EI in N·m².
hints: Write E in pascals: 1 GPa is 10⁹ Pa.
EI is E multiplied by I.
Calculate 200 × 10⁹ × 2 × 10⁻⁶.
questions.onCorrect: 400,000 N·m². EI combines the stiffness of the material with the shape of the section.

misconceptions.feedback: That is EI in kN·m². The question asks in N·m².

questions.prompt: Why must every quantity be in base units before using PL³/3EI?
hints: What happens to L³ if L is in mm instead of m?

acceptedIdeas: Mixed units would scale the result wrongly; base units give the answer in metres.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Mixed units would scale the result wrongly; base units give the answer in metres.. Mixed units scale the result wrongly; base units give δ in metres.

choices.label: Mixed units would scale the result wrongly; base units give the answer in metres.
Because deflection is always measured in pascals.
Because L³ has to be in millimetres.

questions.onCorrect: Base units keep the formula consistent, so δ comes out in metres.

misconceptions.feedback: Deflection is a length. Pascals measure stress and stiffness of material.
The formula works with any consistent set of units, and N, m and Pa are the consistent set.

questions.prompt: A cantilever deflects 5 mm under a 10 kN tip load. Find its stiffness in kN/mm.
hints: Stiffness is load per unit deflection.
Divide the load by the deflection.
Calculate 10 ÷ 5.
questions.onCorrect: 2 kN/mm. Stiffness is load divided by deflection: how much load moves the tip by one unit.

misconceptions.feedback: That is deflection over load, upside down. Stiffness is load per unit deflection.
That multiplies the two. Stiffness divides the load by the deflection.

questions.prompt: A steel cantilever 1 m long (E = 200 GPa, I = 5 × 10⁶ mm⁴) carries 3 kN at its tip. Find the tip deflection in mm.
hints: Find EI in N·m²: E in pascals times I in m⁴.
Divide PL³ by 3EI.
Calculate 3,000 ÷ 3,000,000, then convert to mm.
questions.onCorrect: 1 mm: base units throughout, then metres converted to millimetres.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the deflection in metres. Convert it to mm.
That leaves out EI. Divide PL³ by 3EI.

questions.prompt: A winch lifts a 600 N weight at a steady 2 m/s. How many watts is it delivering?
hints: Power is the work done each second.
Work is force times distance.
Multiply the force by the distance covered each second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each second the winch raises 600 N by 2 m, which is 1,200 J per second: 1,200 W.

questions.onCorrect: 1,200 W. Power is force times speed. For a turning shaft the same idea becomes torque times angular speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides the force by the speed. Power is force times speed.

questions.prompt: Convert 60 rpm to radians per second, to two decimal places.
hints: One revolution is 2π radians.
Divide by 60 to turn minutes into seconds.
Calculate 60 × 2π ÷ 60.
questions.onCorrect: 6.28 rad/s: one turn per second is 2π radians per second.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves the speed in rpm. Multiply by 2π and divide by 60.
That multiplies by 2π but does not divide by 60.

questions.prompt: Why convert 3,000 rpm to radians per second before multiplying by the torque?
hints: What unit of speed makes torque × speed come out in watts?

acceptedIdeas: Watts need the speed in radians per second, not revolutions per minute.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Watts need the speed in radians per second, not revolutions per minute.. Torque in N·m times speed in rad/s gives watts.

choices.label: Watts need the speed in radians per second, not revolutions per minute.
Because rpm is not a measure of speed.
Because torque is measured in radians.

questions.onCorrect: N·m times rad/s gives watts. With rpm the answer would be wrong by a large factor.

misconceptions.feedback: Rpm is a perfectly good speed. It just is not the unit that gives watts.
Torque is in newton metres. The radians belong to the speed.

questions.prompt: Three stages are each 90% efficient. Find the overall efficiency as a percentage.
hints: Each stage passes on a fraction of what it receives.
Multiply the stage efficiencies as decimals.
Calculate 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.9, then convert to a percentage.
questions.onCorrect: 72.9%: each stage keeps 90% of what it gets, so the fractions multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: That subtracts 10% three times. Each stage passes on 90% of what it receives, so multiply.
That is one stage. There are three, and their efficiencies multiply.

questions.prompt: A motor delivers 30 N·m at 600 rpm. Find its power output in watts, to the nearest watt.
hints: Convert rpm to radians per second: multiply by 2π and divide by 60.
Power is torque times angular speed.
Calculate 30 × 600 × 2π ÷ 60 and round.
questions.onCorrect: About 1,885 W: torque times angular speed in radians per second.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies torque by speed in rpm. Convert rpm to radians per second first.

questions.prompt: A lift cable would snap under 100 kN, but it only ever carries 20 kN. How many times stronger is the cable than it needs to be?
hints: What would you divide to compare the strength with the load?
How many times does 20 go into 100?
Count in twenties up to one hundred.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The cable can take 100 kN and carries 20 kN, so it is 100 ÷ 20 = 5 times stronger than needed.

questions.onCorrect: 5 times: strength divided by load. For a single bar, that ratio is its factor of safety.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gap between them. The question asks how many times larger, which is a ratio.
That is the load over the strength, upside down. The cable is stronger than the load.

questions.prompt: Bar A yields at 300 MPa and works at 100 MPa. Bar B yields at 300 MPa and works at 150 MPa. Which has the larger factor of safety?
hints: Divide the yield stress by the working stress for each bar.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Bar A. Dividing 300 by each working stress gives 3 for the first bar and 2 for the second, so the first has the larger factor.

choices.label: Bar A
Bar B
They are the same

questions.onCorrect: Bar A's factor is higher: the same yield stress divided by a smaller working stress.

misconceptions.feedback: A higher working stress leaves less margin, so the factor is smaller.
The yield stresses match, but the working stresses differ, so the factors do too.

questions.prompt: Why is the allowable stress the yield stress divided by the factor of safety?
hints: What is the allowable stress meant to protect against?

acceptedIdeas: It keeps the working stress a safe fraction of the stress that causes failure.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It keeps the working stress a safe fraction of the stress that causes failure.. Dividing by the factor leaves the working stress a safe fraction of the failure stress.

choices.label: It keeps the working stress a safe fraction of the stress that causes failure.
It makes the bar lighter.
Because force and stress are the same thing.

questions.onCorrect: The allowable stress is the highest stress you permit: a safe fraction of the stress that fails the material.

misconceptions.feedback: A lower allowable stress needs more material, so the bar gets heavier, not lighter.
Stress is force per area. They are different quantities.

questions.prompt: A bar of area 200 mm² carries 30 kN. Its steel yields at 240 MPa. Find its factor of safety against yield.
hints: Find the working stress in MPa.
Divide the yield stress by the working stress.
questions.onCorrect: 1.6: the yield stress is 1.6 times the working stress. That is a thin margin for most designs.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the working stress. Divide the yield stress by it.
That is working stress over yield stress, upside down.

questions.prompt: Two people pull a trolley along a straight rail in the same direction, one with 3 kN and one with 4 kN. What is the combined pull, in kN?
hints: Both pull the same way. Do the pulls help each other or fight?
Forces along one line simply combine.
Put the two pulls together.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The pulls act on one line in the same direction, so they add: 3 + 4 = 7 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 7 kN. Pulls along one line in the same direction just add. Pulls at an angle need more care.

misconceptions.feedback: That is 4 − 3. They pull the same way, so they work together.
That multiplies the pulls. Forces on one line combine by adding.

questions.prompt: Which expression gives the vertical component of a force F at angle θ above the horizontal?
hints: Which side of the triangle is opposite the angle?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: F sin θ. The vertical component is the side opposite θ: F sin θ.

choices.label: F sin θ
F cos θ
F tan θ

questions.onCorrect: The vertical side is opposite θ, so it is F sin θ. The side next to the angle gets the cosine.

misconceptions.feedback: F cos θ is the horizontal part, the side that touches the angle.
tan θ is a ratio of two sides, not a share of the force. A component is F times sin θ or cos θ.

questions.prompt: Why is the horizontal part 20 cos 60° and not 20 sin 60°?
hints: Which side of the triangle touches the 60° angle?

acceptedIdeas: The horizontal side touches the angle, so it is the cosine share.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The horizontal side touches the angle, so it is the cosine share.. The horizontal side touches the angle, so it takes the cosine.

choices.label: The horizontal side touches the angle, so it is the cosine share.
Because cos is always the larger of the two.
Because 60° is measured from the vertical.

questions.onCorrect: Cosine goes with the side that touches the angle, whatever its size.

misconceptions.feedback: At 60° the cosine is the smaller one. The choice depends on which side touches the angle.
The angle is measured from the horizontal here, so the horizontal side touches it.

questions.prompt: Which gives the size of the resultant of perpendicular components Rx and Ry?
hints: Think of the two components as the sides of a right-angled triangle.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: √(Rx² + Ry²). The resultant is the hypotenuse: √(Rx² + Ry²).

choices.label: √(Rx² + Ry²)
Rx + Ry
Rx × Ry

questions.onCorrect: The resultant is the long side of the triangle the components make, so Pythagoras applies.

misconceptions.feedback: Adding the sizes only works for forces on one line. At right angles the resultant is shorter.
Multiplying gives units of kN squared, not a force.

questions.prompt: A 26 kN force acts along a line that rises 5 m for every 12 m across. Find its vertical component in kN.
hints: Find the long side of a triangle with sides 5 and 12.
The vertical share is rise over long side.
Calculate 26 × 5 ÷ 13.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The slope triangle 5–12–13 gives sin θ = 5/13, so the vertical component is 26 × 5/13 = 10 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 10 kN: the force times rise over long side, the long side being 13.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the horizontal part, the run over the long side. The vertical part uses the rise.
That is the whole force. Only a share of it acts upward.

questions.prompt: How fast, in rpm, does the second gear turn?
hints: Both gears have the same number of teeth.
Teeth pass the contact point at the same rate on both gears.
Equal gears turn at equal speeds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Equal gears pass teeth at the same rate, so both turn at 100 rpm.

questions.onCorrect: 100 rpm. Same teeth, same speed. Next: what if the teeth differ?

misconceptions.feedback: Neither gear can turn faster than the other when their teeth match.
Nothing slows the second gear. Gears with equal teeth turn at equal rates.

questions.prompt: A 10-tooth driver meshes with a 40-tooth gear. How does the 40-tooth gear turn?
hints: Speed × teeth is equal on both gears. Which has more teeth?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More slowly than the driver. More teeth means fewer turns, so the 40-tooth gear turns more slowly.

choices.label: More slowly than the driver
Faster than the driver
At the same speed as the driver

questions.onCorrect: The gear with more teeth turns more slowly: speed × teeth stays equal.

misconceptions.feedback: A gear with more teeth passes more teeth per turn, so it needs fewer turns to keep pace.
Equal speeds need equal teeth. These gears have different counts.

questions.prompt: A gear pair cuts a shaft's speed to a fifth. By what factor is the torque multiplied, if the mesh is lossless?
hints: An ideal mesh passes on all the power.
Power is torque times speed.
If speed falls by a factor, torque rises by the same factor.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Power = torque × speed is kept, so torque rises by the factor that speed falls: 5.

questions.onCorrect: Five. Power is kept, so a fifth of the speed gives five times the torque.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the speed factor. Torque rises by the factor that speed falls by.
That squares the factor. Torque rises by the same factor as the speed falls.

questions.prompt: Why does the torque rise when the speed falls?
hints: What stays the same across a lossless mesh?

acceptedIdeas: Power is torque × speed, and an ideal mesh keeps the power.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Power is torque × speed, and an ideal mesh keeps the power.. Power is torque times speed and is kept, so slower means more torque.

choices.label: Power is torque × speed, and an ideal mesh keeps the power.
Slower shafts are always heavier.
The teeth add extra torque.

questions.onCorrect: Power is kept, so a slower shaft must carry proportionally more torque.

misconceptions.feedback: Weight is not the reason. The mesh conserves power, and power is torque times speed.
Teeth transfer torque. They do not create any.

questions.prompt: A 15-tooth driver supplies 6 N·m to a 45-tooth gear through a lossless mesh. Find the output torque in N·m.
hints: Find the gear ratio, driven over driver.
Torque rises by the ratio.
Calculate 6 × 45 ÷ 15.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ratio is 45/15 = 3, so the torque is 6 × 3 = 18 N·m.

questions.onCorrect: 18 N·m: torque rises by the gear ratio when speed falls by it.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by the ratio. Torque rises as speed falls.
That is the input torque. A slower output shaft carries more.

questions.prompt: A stuck nut needs a 100 N push on a short spanner. You swap it for a spanner twice as long and still push at the end. What push, in newtons, does the long spanner need?
hints: The nut needs the same turning moment either way.
A moment is force times distance.
Twice the distance needs half the force.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The moment is fixed: 100 N × d. With 2d, the force is 100 ÷ 2 = 50 N.

questions.onCorrect: 50 N. The same turning moment with twice the arm needs half the force. That is the lever.

misconceptions.feedback: A longer spanner means less force, not more, for the same moment.
That is the push with the short spanner. A longer arm needs less force.

questions.prompt: Which gives a lever the greater mechanical advantage?
hints: MA is the effort arm divided by the load arm.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A longer effort arm. MA = effort arm ÷ load arm, so a longer effort arm raises it.

choices.label: A longer effort arm
A longer load arm
A heavier load

questions.onCorrect: MA is effort arm over load arm, so lengthening the effort arm raises it.

misconceptions.feedback: A longer load arm lowers the ratio, since the load arm is the divisor.
The load does not change the ratio of the arms. It changes the effort needed.

questions.prompt: Why do the moments about the fulcrum balance?
hints: What is the net moment on a body at rest?

acceptedIdeas: The lever is held at rest, so its net moment is zero.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The lever is held at rest, so its net moment is zero.. At rest the net moment is zero, so effort × effort arm equals load × load arm.

choices.label: The lever is held at rest, so its net moment is zero.
Because the two arms are always equal.
Because the effort always equals the load.

questions.onCorrect: At rest, the moments cancel about any point. Choosing the fulcrum removes the unknown force there.

misconceptions.feedback: The arms usually differ, and that difference is what gives mechanical advantage.
The effort and load differ too. Only their moments match.

questions.prompt: In tweezers, the effort is applied between the fulcrum and the load. Which class of lever is that?
hints: Which of the three points is in the middle?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Third class. Effort in the middle is a third-class lever.

choices.label: First class
Second class
Third class

questions.onCorrect: Effort in the middle makes a third-class lever, which gives up force for speed and reach.

misconceptions.feedback: First class has the fulcrum in the middle, like a seesaw.
Second class has the load in the middle, like a nutcracker.

questions.prompt: A pulley system has 3 strands supporting the moving block, which carries a 900 N load. Ignoring friction and the block's weight, find the effort in newtons.
hints: The rope tension is the same in every strand.
The supporting strands share the load equally.
Calculate 900 ÷ 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the 3 strands carries the rope tension: effort = 900 ÷ 3 = 300 N.

questions.onCorrect: 300 N: the load divided by the number of supporting strands.

misconceptions.feedback: That multiplies by the number of strands. They share the load, so divide.
That is the load. The strands share it.

questions.prompt: A see-saw balances with a 300 N child sitting 2 m from the pivot on one side. The other child also sits 2 m from the pivot, on the other side. How heavy is that child, in newtons?
hints: Each sits the same distance from the middle.
What would tip the see-saw if the weights differed?
Equal distances need equal weights.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Equal distances from the pivot balance only if the weights are equal, so the other child also weighs 300 N.

questions.onCorrect: 300 N. At equal distances, equal moments need equal weights. Next: what if the distances differ?

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the two weights. Balance needs the two sides to turn the see-saw equally.
Half the weight would only balance at twice the distance. Both children sit the same distance out.

questions.prompt: Which change doubles the moment of a push on a spanner?
hints: M = F × d. Which letter does each option change?

acceptedIdeas: Push at twice the distance from the bolt
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Push at twice the distance from the bolt. Doubling d doubles M = F × d.

choices.label: Push at twice the distance from the bolt
Push with half the force
Push along the handle instead of across it

questions.onCorrect: M = F × d, so doubling the perpendicular distance doubles the moment.

misconceptions.feedback: Half the force halves the moment. Moment is force times distance.
A push along the handle has no distance at right angles to it, so it does not turn the bolt.

questions.prompt: Why does only 90 sin 30° count towards the moment?
hints: Which part of the force could swing the handle round?

acceptedIdeas: Only the part of the force across the spanner turns it.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Only the part of the force across the spanner turns it.. The component along the spanner does not turn it; the component across it does.

choices.label: Only the part of the force across the spanner turns it.
Sine is used for every moment, whatever the angle.
The bolt is only affected by the smaller part of any force.

questions.onCorrect: The part along the handle has no turning effect. Only the part across it does.

misconceptions.feedback: A push at right angles needs no sine at all. Sine appears here because of the angle to the spanner.
Size is not the reason. The part along the handle is a real force but has no turning effect.

questions.prompt: A 60 N force acts on a 0.5 m wrench at 30° to the wrench. Find the moment about the nut in N·m.
hints: Which part of the 60 N acts across the wrench?
That part is 60 × sin 30°.
Multiply it by 0.5 m.
questions.onCorrect: 15 N·m: only the part across the wrench, 60 sin 30°, multiplies the full distance.

misconceptions.feedback: That treats the push as fully at right angles. Only the part across the wrench turns it.
That uses cos 30°, the part along the wrench, which does not turn it.

questions.prompt: A 6 m plank rests on a post at each end, with a 12 kN crate 2 m from the left end. The left post pushes up with 8 kN. Cut the plank 1 m from the left end. What force, in kN, must the cut face supply to keep the left piece still?
hints: The left piece is still, so the forces on it must balance.
What pushes up on it, and is anything pushing down?
The crate is not on this piece.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the post's 8 kN acts on the left piece, so the cut face must supply 8 kN the other way.

questions.onCorrect: 8 kN. Each piece must still balance after the cut, so the cut face supplies the force: the shear force.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole crate, which sits to the right of the cut and is not on the left piece.
That is the right post's push, which acts on the far piece.

questions.prompt: The left reaction is 10 kN upward and nothing else acts on the left piece. What is the shear force at the cut?
hints: Count upward forces on the left piece as positive.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: +10 kN. The only force is 10 kN upward, so V = +10 kN.

choices.label: +10 kN
−10 kN
0 kN

questions.onCorrect: Upward forces on the left piece count positive, so the shear is +10 kN.

misconceptions.feedback: An upward force on the left piece counts positive, so the sign is the other way.
The reaction is on the left piece and nothing cancels it, so the shear is not zero.

questions.prompt: A 5 kN upward force acts on the left piece, 2 m from the cut. Find its moment about the cut in kN·m.
hints: A moment is force times perpendicular distance.
The force is 5 kN and the distance is 2 m.
Multiply them.
questions.onCorrect: 10 kN·m. The bending moment adds up force times distance for every force on the piece.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the force and the distance. A moment multiplies them.
That divides the force by the distance. A moment multiplies them.

questions.prompt: Why is it enough to use only the forces to the left of the cut?
hints: What must be true of both pieces once the beam is cut?

acceptedIdeas: Each piece balances on its own, so either one gives the same moment.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each piece balances on its own, so either one gives the same moment.. Each piece is in equilibrium, so one side's forces give the whole moment.

choices.label: Each piece balances on its own, so either one gives the same moment.
Forces to the right never produce a moment.
The left side of a beam is always the stronger side.

questions.onCorrect: Both pieces are in equilibrium, so one side's forces are enough. Pick the side with fewer forces.

misconceptions.feedback: Forces on the right do have moments about the cut. They simply give the same answer as the ones on the left.
Neither side is stronger. The beam is the same either way.

questions.prompt: An 8 m beam on end supports carries 24 kN at x = 6 m, so the reactions are 6 kN at A and 18 kN at B. Find the shear force just to the right of the load, in kN, counting upward forces on the left piece as positive.
hints: Add the vertical forces on the piece to the left of the cut.
Both the reaction at A and the load are on that piece.
Calculate 6 − 24, keeping the sign.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Left of the cut: +6 kN reaction and −24 kN load, so V = 6 − 24 = −18 kN, which matches B's reaction.

questions.onCorrect: −18 kN. The load outweighs the reaction at A, and the shear equals minus the reaction at B.

misconceptions.feedback: Check the sign: just right of a downward load, upward forces on the left piece are outweighed.
That is the shear just left of the load. Just to its right the load is on the left piece too.

questions.prompt: A 20 kN load hangs from a single steel rod. You replace the rod with two identical rods side by side, sharing the load equally. What force, in kN, does each rod carry?
hints: The two rods share the load equally.
Together they carry the whole 20 kN.
Divide the load between the two rods.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two identical rods share the 20 kN equally, so each carries 20 ÷ 2 = 10 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 10 kN each. Each rod now carries half the force, but it is the force per area that matters.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole load on one rod. The two rods share it.
Two rods do not double the load. Together they carry exactly the load.

questions.prompt: A bar carries a fixed force. Its cross-sectional area is doubled. What happens to the stress?
hints: Stress is force divided by area.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It halves. σ = F/A, so doubling A halves σ.

choices.label: It halves
It doubles
It stays the same

questions.onCorrect: Stress is F/A, so doubling the area halves the stress for the same force.

misconceptions.feedback: Stress is force divided by area, so more area means less stress.
The force is the same, but it is spread over a larger area.

questions.prompt: A 2 m bar stretches by 1 mm. Find its strain, as a plain number.
hints: Strain is extension divided by original length.
Use the same unit for both lengths.
Write 2 m as 2,000 mm.
questions.onCorrect: 0.0005, a pure ratio with no unit. Strain is the stretch as a fraction of the original length.

misconceptions.feedback: That divides by 2 without converting. The lengths must be in the same unit.
That is the length divided by the stretch, upside down.

questions.prompt: Why write 200 GPa as 200,000 MPa?
hints: What happens to the strain if the units of stress and E differ?

acceptedIdeas: Stress and E must share a unit, so that strain comes out as a plain ratio.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Stress and E must share a unit, so that strain comes out as a plain ratio.. Stress and E must share a unit, so 200 GPa becomes 200,000 MPa.

choices.label: Stress and E must share a unit, so that strain comes out as a plain ratio.
Because MPa is the only unit allowed for E.
Because strain is measured in MPa.

questions.onCorrect: Matching units make stress ÷ E a plain ratio. 1 GPa is 1,000 MPa.

misconceptions.feedback: E can be quoted in GPa. The units only need to match the stress in the calculation.
Strain has no unit. It is the ratio of two lengths.

questions.prompt: A steel bar (E = 200 GPa) has a strain of 0.0012. Find the stress in MPa.
hints: In the elastic range, stress is E times strain.
Write E in MPa.
questions.onCorrect: 240 MPa: E times strain, with E in MPa. It is just below this steel's yield stress.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the stress in GPa, from using E = 200. Use E in MPa for a result in MPa.

questions.prompt: A 6 m plank is held up by a post at each end. A 12 kN crate sits exactly halfway along it. How much does each post carry, in kN?
hints: The crate is exactly halfway. Does either post carry more?
The two posts together must carry the whole crate.
Share the crate between the two equally.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The crate is at the middle, so by symmetry each post carries half of 12 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 6 kN each, by symmetry. What if the crate is nearer one end?

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole crate on one post. Symmetry shares it between the two.
That is only a quarter of the crate. The two posts together must carry all of it.

questions.prompt: You take moments about support A. Which unknown force disappears from the equation?
hints: Where does the reaction at A act? How far is that from A?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reaction at A. The reaction at A passes through A, so its moment about A is zero.

choices.label: The reaction at A
The reaction at B
The load

questions.onCorrect: The reaction at A acts through A, so it has no arm and no moment about A.

misconceptions.feedback: The reaction at B acts at a distance from A, so it still has a moment about A.
The load is known, and it acts away from A, so it stays in the equation.

questions.prompt: Why take moments about A?
hints: What is the moment of a force whose line passes through the point?

acceptedIdeas: The reaction at A acts through A, so it drops out and leaves one unknown.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reaction at A acts through A, so it drops out and leaves one unknown.. The reaction at A passes through A, so it has no moment and drops out.

choices.label: The reaction at A acts through A, so it drops out and leaves one unknown.
Moments can only be taken about the left support.
The load always acts at A.

questions.onCorrect: Choose the point so that an unknown force passes through it. That leaves one unknown.

misconceptions.feedback: Moments can be taken about any point. The skill is choosing the one that removes an unknown.
The load here sits at x = 1 m, not at A.

questions.prompt: A load of 5 kN/m covers 4 m of a beam, starting at x = 0. Which single force replaces it when finding reactions?
hints: Total = intensity × length. Where is the middle of the loaded length?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 20 kN at x = 2 m. 5 × 4 = 20 kN, acting at the middle of the loaded length, x = 2 m.

choices.label: 20 kN at x = 2 m
20 kN at x = 4 m
5 kN at x = 2 m

questions.onCorrect: The total is intensity times length, acting at the middle of the loaded length.

misconceptions.feedback: The force acts at the middle of the loaded length, not at its end.
That is the intensity. The total multiplies it by the loaded length.

questions.prompt: A 10 m beam on end supports carries 3 kN/m over its whole length. Find the left reaction in kN.
hints: What is the total of the spread load?
Where does the replacement force act?
The load is centred, so the supports share it equally.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The load totals 3 × 10 = 30 kN at the middle, so each support carries half: 15 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 15 kN. The spread load acts as 30 kN at the middle, shared equally by symmetry.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole load. Each support takes a share.
That is a quarter of the load. Each support carries half.

questions.prompt: A symmetrical triangular truss carries a 12 kN load at its apex and rests on two supports, one under each foot. What force, in kN, does each support carry?
hints: The truss is symmetrical and the load is at the middle.
Together the two supports carry the whole load.
Divide the load between the two supports.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The supports share the 12 kN load equally, so each carries 12 ÷ 2 = 6 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 6 kN each. A symmetrical load is shared equally between the supports.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole load on one support. The two supports share it.
Two supports do not double the load. Together they carry exactly the load.

questions.prompt: A rope holds up a hanging lamp. Is the rope in tension or compression?
hints: Is the rope being stretched or squashed?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Tension. The rope is stretched along its length, so it is in tension.

choices.label: Tension
Compression

questions.onCorrect: The rope is pulled along its length, so it is in tension. A member that is pushed is in compression.

misconceptions.feedback: Compression squashes a member. A rope that holds something up is being stretched.

questions.prompt: Why is there a factor of 2 in 2 × F × 4/5 = 24?
hints: How many members meet at the apex joint?

acceptedIdeas: Two sloping members meet at the apex and each gives an equal vertical part.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two sloping members meet at the apex and each gives an equal vertical part.. Two members meet at the apex, each giving a vertical part of F × 4/5.

choices.label: Two sloping members meet at the apex and each gives an equal vertical part.
The load is counted twice, once for each support.
Each member carries double its own vertical part.

questions.onCorrect: Each member that meets the joint adds its own vertical part, and two meet at the apex.

misconceptions.feedback: The load is counted once. The 2 counts the members meeting at the joint.
A member's vertical part is its force times rise over length, not double it.

questions.prompt: A truss spans 6 m with its apex 4 m high, so each sloping member is 5 m long. A 32 kN load hangs at the apex. Find the force in each sloping member in kN.
hints: Isolate the apex joint.
Two members each give a vertical part of F × 4/5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: At the apex 2F × 4/5 = 32, so F = 32 ÷ 1.6 = 20 kN.

questions.onCorrect: 20 kN. Two members share the load, and each gives only 4/5 of its force upward.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the whole load. Two members share it, and each is slanted.
That is each member's vertical share. The member itself carries more because it slants.

question.prompt: A Warren truss has bottom joints A, D and B 3 m apart and top joints C and E 2 m up, so each diagonal is 2.5 m long. A 16 kN load hangs from D. Find the size of the force in the top member CE in kN.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each reaction is 8 kN. At A: F_AC × 2/2.5 = 8, so AC = 10 kN compression. At C, CD balances AC vertically (10 kN tension) and CE = 10 × 1.5/2.5 × 2 = 12 kN compression.
